chapters.title: Chapter XII
paragraphs: While Miss Linton wandered miserably through the park and garden, always silent and nearly always crying, her brother shut himself away with books he never opened. I imagined he was wearing himself out waiting for Catherine to regret her behaviour, come of her own accord to ask forgiveness, and make peace. Meanwhile, _she_ stubbornly refused to eat, probably imagining that at every meal Edgar was almost choking over her absence, and that only pride stopped him from rushing to throw himself at her feet. I went about my work convinced that there was only one sensible person inside the Grange, and that person was me. I wasted no sympathy on Miss Isabella, no arguments on my mistress, and very little attention on my master's sighs. Since he could not hear his wife's voice, he longed at least to hear her name. As far as I was concerned, they could sort themselves out however they liked. It was a tiresomely slow business, but eventually I began to welcome what seemed to be the first faint sign of progress—or so I thought at first.

On the third day Mrs. Linton unbolted her door. She had emptied both her water jug and her decanter, and asked for more water and a bowl of gruel, saying she believed she was dying. I took this to be a speech intended for Edgar. I believed nothing of the sort, so I kept it to myself and brought her tea and dry toast. She ate and drank eagerly, then fell back against her pillow, clenching her hands and groaning. “Oh, I will die,” she cried, “since nobody cares anything about me. I wish I hadn't eaten that.” Much later I heard her mutter, “No, I won't die—he'd be pleased—he doesn't love me at all—he would never miss me!”
“Did you need anything, ma'am?” I asked. I still kept an outward appearance of calm, despite her deathly face and her strange, overblown behaviour.
“What is that unfeeling creature doing?” she demanded, pushing the thick tangles of hair away from her shrunken face. “Has he sunk into a stupor, or is he dead?”
“Neither, if you mean Mr. Linton,” I answered. “I think he's fairly well, although he spends rather too much time studying. He's always with his books, as he has no other company.”
Had I understood how ill she really was, I would never have said that. But I could not shake off my belief that some of her illness was an act.

“With his books!” she cried in disbelief. “And I'm dying! I'm at the edge of the grave! My God! Does he know how I've changed?” She stared at herself in the mirror on the opposite wall. “Is that Catherine Linton? He thinks I'm sulking—perhaps only playing. Can't you tell him this is terribly serious? Nelly, if it isn't too late, once I know how he feels I'll choose between two things: either starve myself straight away—which would be no punishment to him unless he had a heart—or recover and leave the country. Are you telling me the truth about him? Be careful. Does he really care so little whether I live?”
“Why, ma'am,” I said, “the master has no idea that your mind is disturbed. Naturally he doesn't fear that you'll let yourself die of hunger.”
“You don't think so? Can't you tell him I will?” she replied. “Make him believe it! Tell him it's your own opinion: say you're certain I will!”
“No, Mrs. Linton, you're forgetting,” I pointed out, “that you ate quite heartily this evening. Tomorrow you'll feel the benefit of it.”

“If only I knew it would kill him,” she broke in, “I'd kill myself this instant! Through these three dreadful nights I haven't closed my eyes—and oh, how I've suffered! I've been haunted, Nelly! But I'm beginning to think you don't like me. How strange! I thought that even if everyone hated and despised one another, they couldn't help loving me. And in a few hours they've all become my enemies. _They_ have, I'm sure of it—the people _here_. How miserable to die with all their cold faces round me! Isabella, frightened and disgusted, not daring to enter the room because watching Catherine die would be so dreadful. And Edgar standing solemnly by, waiting for it to end; then thanking God for bringing peace back to his house, and going back to his _books_! In the name of everything that has a feeling heart, what business has he with _books_ while I'm dying?”

She could not endure the picture I had planted in her mind of Mr. Linton calmly accepting her fate. She tossed about until her feverish confusion became frenzy, and tore her pillow with her teeth. Then she sat up, burning hot, and asked me to open the window. It was the middle of winter, with a strong wind from the northeast, and I refused. The expressions passing across her face and her sudden changes of mood now frightened me badly. I remembered her earlier illness and the doctor's warning that we must not oppose her. A moment before she had been violent; now she propped herself on one arm and seemed quite unaware of my refusal. Like a child playing, she pulled feathers through the holes she had torn and arranged them on the sheet according to the birds they came from. Her thoughts had wandered elsewhere.

“That's from a turkey,” she murmured to herself, “and this is a wild duck's, and this a pigeon's. Ah, they've put pigeon's feathers in the pillows—no wonder I couldn't die! I must remember to throw it on the floor when I lie down. And here's a moor-cock's; and this one—I'd know it among a thousand—it's a lapwing's. A bonny bird, circling above our heads out in the middle of the moor. It wanted to reach its nest: the clouds had come down on the hills and it could feel rain coming. We picked this feather up from the heather; nobody shot the bird. In winter we found its nest full of little skeletons. Heathcliff had set a trap over it, and the parents dared not come back. Afterwards I made him promise never to shoot a lapwing, and he never did. Yes, here are more! Did he shoot my lapwings, Nelly? Are any of them red? Let me see.”

“Stop that childish nonsense!” I interrupted, pulling the pillow away and turning the holes towards the mattress, for she was emptying it by the handful. “Lie down and close your eyes. Your mind is wandering. What a mess! The down's blowing about like snow.”
I moved around the room gathering it up.

“When I look at you, Nelly,” she continued dreamily, “I see an old woman, with grey hair and bent shoulders. This bed is the fairy cave beneath Penistone Crags, and you're collecting elf-bolts to harm our heifers. While I'm here you pretend they're only scraps of wool. That's what you'll be in fifty years: I know you're not like that now. My mind isn't wandering; you're wrong. Otherwise I'd believe you really _were_ that shrivelled witch, and that I _was_ under Penistone Crags. But I know it's night, and there are two candles on the table, making the black cupboard shine like jet.”
“The black cupboard? Where?” I asked. “You're talking in your sleep!”
“Against the wall, where it always is,” she answered. “It _does_ look strange—there's a face in it!”
“There isn't a cupboard in this room, and there never has been,” I said. I sat down again, fastening back the curtain so I could watch her.
“Can't _you_ see that face?” she asked, staring hard into the mirror.
Nothing I said could make her understand that it was her own face. At last I got up and covered the mirror with a shawl.
“It's still behind there!” she went on anxiously. “And it moved. Who is it? I hope it won't come out when you've gone! Oh! Nelly, this room is haunted! I'm afraid to be left alone!”
I held her hand and told her to be calm. One shudder after another shook her whole body, and she kept insisting on staring towards the mirror.
“There's nobody here!” I told her firmly. “It was _you_, Mrs. Linton. A little while ago you knew that.”
“Me!” she gasped. “And the clock's striking twelve! Then it's true! How dreadful!”
She gripped the bedclothes and pulled them over her eyes. I tried to slip to the door to call her husband, but a piercing scream brought me back: the shawl had fallen off the mirror.
“Why, what _is_ wrong?” I cried. “Who's the coward now? Wake up! That's the looking-glass—the mirror, Mrs. Linton. You're seeing yourself, and there I am beside you.”
She clung to me, trembling and confused. Gradually, though, the terror left her face, and a flush of shame replaced its deathly pallor.

“Oh, dear! I thought I was at home,” she sighed. “I thought I was lying in my own room at Wuthering Heights. I'm so weak that my head got muddled, and I screamed without knowing what I was doing. Don't say anything; just stay with me. I'm afraid to sleep. My dreams terrify me.”
“A good sleep would help you, ma'am,” I replied. “And I hope all this suffering will stop you from trying to starve yourself again.”

“Oh, if only I were in my own bed in the old house!” she went on bitterly, wringing her hands. “With the wind sounding through the fir trees outside the window. Let me feel it—it blows straight down from the moor—please let me have one breath!”

To soothe her, I opened the casement a little for a few seconds. An icy gust swept in; I shut it and went back to her side. Now she lay still, her face streaming with tears. Physical exhaustion had completely broken her spirit. Our fiery Catherine had become no stronger than a crying child.
“How long have I been shut in here?” she asked, suddenly rousing herself.
“You shut yourself in on Monday evening,” I answered, “and now it's Thursday night—or rather, Friday morning.”
“What! In the same week?” she cried. “Has it only been that little time?”
“Long enough to live on nothing but cold water and bad temper,” I remarked.

“Well, it seems such a weary stretch of hours,” she muttered uncertainly. “It must be longer. I remember being in the parlour after their quarrel, and Edgar provoking me cruelly, and rushing into this room in despair. The moment I bolted the door everything went black, and I fell to the floor. I couldn't explain to Edgar how certain I was that I'd have a fit, or go raving mad, if he kept tormenting me! I couldn't control my tongue or my thoughts. Perhaps he didn't understand my agony: I barely had enough sense left to try to escape him and his voice. By the time I could see and hear properly again, dawn was breaking. Nelly, I'll tell you what I thought then, and what has come back again and again until I've feared for my sanity. As I lay with my head against that table leg, barely able to make out the grey square of the window, I thought I was inside the oak-panelled bed at home. My heart ached with some terrible grief which I couldn't remember just after waking. I lay thinking and tormenting myself, trying to discover what it was; and, strangest of all, the last seven years of my life had vanished! I couldn't remember their ever happening. I was a child; my father had just been buried, and I was miserable because Hindley had ordered Heathcliff and me to be separated. For the first time I had been put to sleep alone. After a night of crying I woke from a wretched doze and raised my hand to slide back the panels. It hit the tabletop! I swept it across the carpet, and then my memory came flooding back. My first grief disappeared beneath a convulsion of despair. I can't explain why I felt so desperately miserable. I must have been out of my mind for a moment, because there's hardly any reason for it. But imagine that, at twelve years old, I had been torn away from the Heights, from everything I'd known as a child, and from the person who was everything to me—as Heathcliff was then—and changed in a single instant into Mrs. Linton, mistress of Thrushcross Grange and wife to a stranger. From then on, an exile and an outcast from everything that had been my world. That may give you some idea of the pit I was crawling in! Shake your head all you like, Nelly: _you've_ helped to drive me out of my senses! You should have spoken to Edgar—you really should—and made him leave me in peace! Oh, I'm burning! I wish I were outside! I wish I were a girl again, half wild and tough and free, laughing at injuries instead of going mad over them! Why have I changed so much? Why do a few words send my blood into such hellish turmoil? I'm sure I'd be myself again if I could get among the heather on those hills. Open the window again, wide, and fasten it back! Hurry—why don't you move?”
“Because I won't let you catch your death of cold,” I answered.
“You mean you won't give me a chance to live,” she said sullenly. “Well, I'm not helpless yet. I'll open it myself.”

Before I could stop her she slid out of bed, staggered across the room, flung the window open, and leaned out. She took no notice of the freezing air cutting round her shoulders like a knife. I begged her to come away and finally tried to pull her back. But I soon found that the strength of her delirium was far greater than mine. Her later words and actions convinced me that she _was_ delirious. There was no moon; below us everything lay in a dark mist. Not a light shone from a house, near or far: they had all been put out long before. The lights of Wuthering Heights could never be seen from there in any case, yet she insisted she could see them shining.

“Look!” she cried eagerly. “That's my room, with the candle burning and the trees waving in front of it. The other candle's in Joseph's attic. Joseph stays up late, doesn't he? He's waiting for me to come home so he can lock the gate. Well, he'll have to wait a while longer. It's a hard journey, with a sad heart to make it, and we must go past Gimmerton church along the way! We've often faced its ghosts together, daring each other to stand among the graves and call them out. But, Heathcliff, if I dare you now, will you come? If you do, I'll keep you. I won't lie there alone. They can bury me twelve feet deep and bring the church down on top of me, but I won't rest until you're with me. I never will!”

She stopped, then went on with a strange smile. “He's thinking it over—he'd rather I came to him! Find a way, then! Not through that churchyard. How slow you are! Be satisfied; you've always followed me!”

I saw that arguing with her madness was useless. I was trying to work out how to reach something to wrap round her without letting go of her—for I dared not leave her alone at that wide-open window—when, to my dismay, the door handle rattled and Mr. Linton came in. He had only just left the library. As he passed along the hall, he had heard our voices and been drawn by curiosity, or fear, to find out what we were doing up at such an hour.

“Oh, sir!” I cried, cutting short the exclamation that rose to his lips at the sight before him and the bitter cold of the room. “My poor mistress is ill, and she's too much for me. I can't manage her at all. Please come and persuade her to go to bed. Put your anger aside: it's hard to guide her any way except the one she chooses.”
“Catherine ill?” he said, hurrying towards us. “Close the window, Ellen! Catherine! Why—”
He stopped. The sight of Mrs. Linton's wasted face struck him speechless. He could only look from her to me in horrified astonishment.

“She has been upsetting herself in here,” I continued, “and hardly eating, without making any complaint. She wouldn't let any of us in until this evening, so we couldn't tell you how she was, because we didn't know ourselves. But it's nothing.”

I knew my explanations sounded clumsy. The master frowned. “Nothing, is it, Ellen Dean?” he said sternly. “You'll give me a better explanation for keeping me in ignorance of this!” He took his wife in his arms and gazed at her in anguish.

At first she showed no sign of knowing him. Her distracted eyes seemed unable to see him at all. But the delirium did not hold her continuously. Once her eyes had been drawn away from the darkness outside, her attention slowly settled on him, and she realised who was holding her.

“Ah! So you've come, Edgar Linton?” she said, suddenly fierce. “You're one of those creatures who always turn up when they're least wanted, and never when they are! I suppose we'll have plenty of weeping now—I can see we will—but that won't keep me from my narrow home out there, my resting place, where I'll be before spring is over! There it is: not with the Lintons under the chapel roof, mind you, but outside in the open air, with a headstone. You can choose for yourself whether to go to them or come to me!”
“Catherine, what have you done?” the master began. “Do I mean nothing to you any more? Do you love that wretch Heath—”

“Be quiet!” cried Mrs. Linton. “Quiet, this instant! Say that name and I'll settle everything by jumping from the window! You can have what you're touching now, but before you touch me again my soul will be on that hilltop. I don't want you, Edgar. I'm beyond wanting you. Go back to your books. I'm glad you have something to comfort you, because everything you had in me is gone.”
“Her mind is wandering, sir,” I put in. “She's been talking nonsense all evening. Give her peace and proper care, and she'll recover. From now on we must be careful how we upset her.”

“I want no more advice from you,” Mr. Linton answered. “You knew what your mistress was like, and you encouraged me to torment her. And you gave me no hint of her condition in all these three days! It was heartless! Months of illness couldn't have changed her this much!”

I started to defend myself. It seemed too much to be blamed for someone else's wicked wilfulness. “I knew Mrs. Linton was stubborn and domineering,” I cried, “but I didn't know you wanted me to encourage her violent temper! I didn't know I was meant to turn a blind eye to Mr. Heathcliff just to humour her. I did my duty as a loyal servant by telling you, and now I've had a loyal servant's reward! Well, I'll know to be more careful next time. Next time you can find things out for yourself!”
“The next time you bring me tales, Ellen Dean, you will leave my service,” he replied.

“So you would rather hear nothing about it, Mr. Linton?” I said. “Heathcliff has your permission to court Miss Isabella, and to drop in whenever you're away, for the express purpose of turning my mistress against you?”
Confused though Catherine was, she quickly understood how our conversation concerned her.

“Ah! Nelly has betrayed me,” she cried furiously. “Nelly is my secret enemy. You witch! So you really are gathering elf-bolts to hurt us! Let me go, and I'll make her regret it! I'll make her scream that she takes it back!”

Mad fury blazed in her eyes. She fought desperately to free herself from Linton's arms. I had no wish to stay and see what happened. Deciding to take responsibility myself for getting medical help, I left the room.

As I crossed the garden towards the road, I noticed something white moving near a bridle hook fixed into the wall. Its jerky movements were plainly caused by something other than the wind. Despite my hurry, I stopped to examine it: otherwise I knew my imagination might forever insist I had seen something from the other world. To my great surprise and bewilderment, I discovered, more by touch than sight, that Miss Isabella's spaniel, Fanny, was hanging by a handkerchief and almost at its last breath. I quickly freed the animal and lifted it into the garden. I had seen it follow its mistress upstairs when she went to bed, and could not imagine how it had got outside or who had been cruel enough to do this. While I was undoing the knot round the hook, I thought I repeatedly heard horses galloping some distance away. But there was so much else on my mind that I barely thought about it, strange as the sound was in that place at two in the morning.

Fortunately, as I came up the village street, Mr. Kenneth was just leaving his house to visit a patient. My account of Catherine Linton's illness persuaded him to return with me at once. He was a blunt, rough man, and did not hesitate to say he doubted she would survive this second attack unless she followed his instructions more willingly than she had before.

“Nelly Dean,” he said, “I can't help thinking there's something more behind this. What's been happening at the Grange? We've heard some strange reports up here. A strong, healthy lass like Catherine doesn't fall ill over nothing—and people of that sort shouldn't, either. Getting them through a fever and suchlike is hard work. How did it start?”

“The master will tell you,” I answered. “But you know what violent tempers the Earnshaws have, and Mrs. Linton is worse than any of them. I can tell you this much: it began with a quarrel. In the middle of a furious rage she had some kind of fit. At least that's what she says, because she rushed off at the height of it and locked herself away. Afterwards she wouldn't eat, and now she goes from raving to a sort of half-dream. She knows the people round her, but her head is full of strange ideas and things she imagines.”
“Mr. Linton will be upset?” Kenneth asked.
“Upset? If anything happens to her, his heart will break!” I answered. “Don't frighten him any more than you must.”
“Well, I warned him to be careful,” my companion said. “He'll have to bear the consequences of ignoring me! Hasn't he been on friendly terms with Mr. Heathcliff lately?”

“Heathcliff often visits the Grange,” I replied, “though that's more because my mistress knew him as a boy than because the master enjoys his company. Just now he has been relieved of the trouble of calling, after showing some presumptuous intentions towards Miss Linton. I very much doubt he'll be welcomed back.”
“And does Miss Linton give him the cold shoulder?” was the doctor's next question.
“She doesn't confide in me,” I replied, unwilling to discuss it further.

“No, she's a sly one,” he said, shaking his head. “She keeps her secrets! But she's a proper little fool. I've heard from a reliable source that last night—and a fine night it was for it!—she and Heathcliff walked for more than two hours in the plantation behind your house. He urged her not to go back inside, but to get on his horse and ride away with him! The person who told me said she could only put him off by giving her word of honour that she'd be ready the next time they met. When that was to be, he didn't hear. But you tell Mr. Linton to keep his eyes open!”

This news filled me with fresh alarm. I hurried ahead of Kenneth and ran most of the way home. The little dog was still yelping in the garden. I stopped a moment to open the gate for it, but instead of going to the house it raced about sniffing the grass, and would have escaped into the road if I had not caught it and carried it inside. Upstairs, Isabella's empty bedroom confirmed my suspicions. Had I been a few hours earlier, Mrs. Linton's illness might have stopped her from taking this rash step. But what could be done now? There was a faint chance of catching them if someone went after them at once. _I_ could not go, however, and I dared not wake the household and throw everyone into confusion. Still less could I tell my master: he was entirely taken up with his present trouble, with no strength left to bear another grief! I could see no choice but to hold my tongue and let events take their course. Kenneth had now arrived, and I went to announce him, scarcely able to compose my face. Catherine was sleeping uneasily. Her husband had managed to calm the worst of her frenzy and now bent over her pillow, watching every passing expression on her painfully expressive face.

After examining her himself, the doctor told him hopefully that she might recover if we could keep everything around her perfectly and continuously peaceful. To me he indicated that the greatest danger was not so much death as the permanent loss of her reason.

Neither Mr. Linton nor I closed our eyes that night. Indeed, neither of us went to bed. All the servants were up long before their usual time, moving quietly through the house and whispering whenever their work brought them together. Everyone was busy except Miss Isabella, and they began to comment on how soundly she was sleeping. Her brother also asked whether she was up. He seemed impatient for her to appear, and hurt that she showed so little concern for her sister-in-law. I trembled lest he send me to call her, but I was spared the pain of being the first to announce her flight. One of the maids, a thoughtless girl sent on an early errand to Gimmerton, came panting upstairs, burst open-mouthed into the bedroom, and cried, “Oh, dear, dear! What shall we have next? Master, master, our young lady—”
“Stop that noise!” I cried at once, furious at her shouting.
“Lower your voice, Mary. What's happened?” Mr. Linton said. “What's wrong with your young lady?”
“She's gone, she's gone! That Heathcliff's run off wi' her!” the girl gasped.
“That's not true!” Linton cried, getting up in distress. “It can't be. Where did you get such an idea? Ellen Dean, go and find her. It's unbelievable. It cannot be.”
While speaking, he took the maid to the door and again demanded to know what grounds she had for saying such a thing.

“Well, I met the lad who brings milk here on the road,” she stammered, “and he asked if there wasn't trouble at the Grange. I thought he meant the mistress being ill, so I said yes. Then he says, ‘Someone's gone after them, I suppose?’ I stared at him. He saw I knew nowt about it, and told me a gentleman and a lady had stopped to have a horseshoe fixed at a smithy's two miles beyond Gimmerton, not long after midnight! The blacksmith's daughter got up to see who they were, and knew them both straight away. She saw the man—it was Heathcliff, she was certain; besides, nobody could mistake him—put a sovereign into her father's hand to pay him. The lady had her cloak pulled round her face, but she asked for a drink of water. When she drank, the cloak fell back and the lass saw her quite plainly. Heathcliff held both bridles as they rode on. They headed away from the village as fast as those rough roads would let them. The lass didn't tell her father anything, but this morning she's told it all round Gimmerton.”

For appearances' sake I ran to look into Isabella's room, then came back and confirmed the maid's story. Mr. Linton had sat down beside the bed again. When I entered, he looked up, understood from my blank face, and lowered his eyes without a word or an instruction.
“Shall we try to catch them and bring her back?” I asked. “What should we do?”

“She left of her own free will,” the master answered. “She had a right to leave if she chose. Don't trouble me about her again. From now on she's my sister only in name—not because I've disowned her, but because she has disowned me.”

That was everything he said about it. He asked no further questions and never mentioned her again, except to tell me to send whatever belongings she had left in the house to her new home, wherever it might be, once I knew the address.

chapters.title: Chapter XIII
paragraphs: The runaways stayed away for two months. During that time Mrs. Linton endured and survived the worst of what they called a brain fever. No mother could have nursed her only child more devotedly than Edgar nursed her. He watched over her day and night, patiently bearing every trial that her raw nerves and disturbed mind could inflict. Kenneth said that the life he was saving would repay his care only with endless anxiety; in effect, he was sacrificing his own health and strength to preserve the wreck of a human being. But when Catherine was declared out of danger, Edgar's gratitude and joy knew no bounds. Hour after hour he sat beside her, watching her physical health slowly return and encouraging his all-too-hopeful heart with the belief that her mind would regain its balance too, and that she would soon be entirely herself again.

She first left her bedroom at the beginning of the following March. That morning Mr. Linton had laid a handful of golden crocuses on her pillow. When she woke, her eyes, so long without a spark of pleasure, caught sight of them and lit up with delight as she eagerly gathered them together.

“These are the first flowers to come out at the Heights,” she cried. “They make me think of gentle winds bringing a thaw, and warm sunshine, and snow almost melted away. Edgar, isn't the wind from the south? Hasn't most of the snow gone?”

“It's all gone down here, darling,” her husband replied. “I can see only two white patches on the whole sweep of the moors. The sky is blue, the larks are singing, and all the little streams are full to the brim. Catherine, at this time last spring I was longing to have you under this roof. Now I wish you were a mile or two up in those hills. The air is so sweet that I feel sure it would cure you.”

“I'll only go there once more,” the sick woman said. “Then you'll leave me, and I'll stay for ever. Next spring you'll be longing again to have me under this roof, and you'll look back and think you were happy today.”

Linton showered her with tender caresses and tried to cheer her with the most loving words. But she gazed vaguely at the flowers, letting tears gather on her lashes and run down her cheeks without noticing. We knew she really was improving, so we decided that much of her sadness came from being shut in one room for so long, and that a change of scene might help. The master told me to light a fire in the parlour, unused for weeks, and put an easy chair in the sunshine by the window. Then he carried her downstairs. She sat for a long time enjoying the comforting warmth, and, as we had hoped, the things around her revived her spirits. They were familiar, but free from the dreary associations of the sickroom she hated. By evening she seemed utterly worn out, yet nothing could persuade her to return there. I had to make up a bed on the parlour sofa until another room could be prepared. To save her the strain of climbing up and down the stairs, we fitted out this room, where you're lying now, on the same floor as the parlour. Soon she could walk from one to the other, leaning on Edgar's arm. Ah, I thought, with such care she might recover after all. And we had a double reason for wanting it, since another life depended on hers. We hoped that before long the birth of an heir would bring happiness to Mr. Linton and keep his lands from falling into a stranger's grasp.

I should mention that about six weeks after leaving, Isabella sent her brother a short note announcing her marriage to Heathcliff. It seemed cold and stiff, but at the bottom she had added a few faint words in pencil: an uncertain apology and a plea that, if she had offended him, he would remember her kindly and make peace. She insisted that she could not help what she had done at the time, and that now it was done she could not undo it. I believe Linton sent no answer. Two weeks later I received a long letter myself, a strange one, I thought, for a bride just back from her honeymoon. I'll read it to you; I still keep it. Anything left by the dead is precious when we loved them in life.

DEAR ELLEN, it begins,—I arrived at Wuthering Heights last night and heard for the first time that Catherine has been very ill, and still is. I suppose I mustn't write to her, and my brother is either too angry or too upset to answer my note. Yet I must write to someone, and you are the only person left.

Tell Edgar I would give the world to see his face again. Within twenty-four hours of leaving, my heart had returned to Thrushcross Grange, and it is there now, full of affection for him and for Catherine! _But I cannot follow it_—those words are underlined. They mustn't expect me, and they may draw whatever conclusions they please, provided they blame neither weakness of will nor any lack of love in me.

The rest of this letter is for you alone. I have two questions to ask. First, how did you manage to keep the ordinary feelings of a human being while you lived here? I can find no feeling at all that I share with the people around me.

My second question matters very much to me: is Mr. Heathcliff a man? If he is, is he mad? If he isn't, is he a devil? I won't tell you why I ask, but I beg you to explain, if you can, what I have married. Explain when you come to see me; you must come, Ellen, very soon. Don't write. Come yourself, and bring me something from Edgar.

Now I will tell you how I was welcomed into my new home, for I am led to understand that the Heights is to be my home. I dwell on such things as the absence of comforts only to distract myself. They never trouble my thoughts except at the moment I feel their lack. I would laugh and dance with joy if those were all my troubles, and everything else only a monstrous dream!

The sun was setting behind the Grange when we turned on to the moors, so I supposed it was six o'clock. My companion stopped for half an hour to examine the park and gardens, and probably the house itself, as closely as he could. It was therefore dark when we dismounted in the farmhouse's paved yard. Your old fellow servant Joseph came out to welcome us with a tallow candle. His courtesy did him great credit. First he lifted his light to my face, squinted at me spitefully, stuck out his lower lip, and turned away. Then he took both horses to the stables, coming back to lock the outer gate as though we lived in an ancient castle.

Heathcliff stayed outside to speak to him, and I went into the kitchen, a dark, filthy hole. It has changed so much since you looked after it that I doubt you would recognise it. A rough little boy stood by the fire, sturdy and dirty, with something of Catherine in his eyes and round his mouth.
“This is Edgar's nephew by marriage,” I thought, “and in a way mine too. I must shake his hand—and yes, I must kiss him. We ought to be on good terms from the beginning.”
I went up to him and tried to take his plump little fist. “How are you, my dear?” I said.
He answered in a jumble of words I could not understand.
“Shall we be friends, Hareton, you and I?” I tried again.
My persistence earned me a curse and a threat to set Throttler on me if I didn't “get away”.
“Hey, Throttler, lad!” the little wretch whispered, waking a mongrel bulldog in the corner. “Now then, wilt thou be going?” he demanded.

Wanting to stay alive, I obeyed. I stepped outside to wait for the others. Mr. Heathcliff was nowhere to be seen. I followed Joseph to the stables and asked him to come into the house with me. After staring at me and muttering to himself, he wrinkled his nose and said, “Mim! Mim! Mim! Did ever a Christian soul hear owt like it? Such mincing and mumbling! How am I to know what ye're saying?”
“I said I want you to come into the house with me!” I shouted, thinking he must be deaf, though thoroughly disgusted by his rudeness.

“Not me! I've summat else to do,” he answered, and went on working. All the while he worked his long jaws and studied my clothes and face with utter contempt. My clothes were much too fine, but my face, I am certain, was as miserable as he could have wished.

I went round the yard and through a small gate to another door. There I ventured to knock, hoping some more civil servant might appear. After a short wait, a tall, gaunt man opened it. He wore no neckcloth and was otherwise extremely untidy. Shaggy hair hung to his shoulders and almost hid his face. _His_ eyes, too, were like Catherine's, but a ghostly Catherine with every trace of beauty destroyed.
“What do you want here?” he demanded harshly. “Who are you?”
“My name _was_ Isabella Linton,” I replied. “You've seen me before, sir. I've recently married Mr. Heathcliff, and he has brought me here—with your permission, I suppose.”
“So he's back, is he?” asked the recluse, glaring like a starving wolf.
“Yes, we arrived just now,” I said. “But he left me at the kitchen door. When I tried to go inside, your little boy stood guard and frightened me away with a bulldog.”

“A good thing the hellish villain kept his word!” growled my host-to-be. He peered into the darkness behind me, expecting to see Heathcliff, then launched into a stream of curses and threats about what he would have done if the “fiend” had tricked him.

I regretted trying this second door and almost slipped away before he had finished swearing. But before I could do so, he ordered me inside, shut the door, and fastened it again. A large fire gave the huge room its only light. The floor had become uniformly grey; the pewter dishes that used to catch my eye with their brightness when I was a girl were equally dull with tarnish and dust. I asked if I might call the maid and be shown to a bedroom! Mr. Earnshaw did not trouble to answer. He walked up and down with his hands in his pockets, apparently forgetting I was there. He seemed so deeply lost in thought, and looked so hostile to all humanity, that I shrank from disturbing him again.

You won't be surprised, Ellen, that I felt especially miserable, sitting in something worse than solitude beside that unwelcoming hearth. Only four miles away lay my lovely home, with the only people in the world I loved. Yet the Atlantic might as well have separated us: I could not cross those four miles! I asked myself where I could turn for comfort. And—don't tell Edgar or Catherine this—one sorrow rose above all the rest: despair at finding nobody who could or would stand beside me against Heathcliff! I had almost welcomed the prospect of shelter at Wuthering Heights because it would save me from living alone with him. But he knew the people we were coming to, and had no fear of their interfering.

I sat thinking miserably for a long time. The clock struck eight, then nine, while my companion still paced up and down with his head sunk on his chest. He said nothing, except when an occasional groan or bitter exclamation escaped him. I listened for a woman's voice somewhere in the house. In between I tormented myself with regrets and dread of the future, until I could no longer keep from sighing and crying aloud. I didn't realise how openly I was grieving until Earnshaw stopped in front of me during his steady pacing and stared with newly awakened surprise. Seizing the chance now that I had his attention, I cried, “I'm tired from travelling, and I want to go to bed! Where's the maid? Show me where to find her, since she won't come to me!”
“We haven't got one,” he answered. “You'll have to look after yourself!”
“Where am I to sleep, then?” I sobbed. Weariness and misery had crushed every concern for my dignity.
“Joseph will show you Heathcliff's room,” he said. “Open that door. He's in there.”
I was about to obey when he suddenly stopped me and added in the strangest voice, “Be sure to turn the key and bolt your door. Don't forget!”
“Very well!” I said. “But why, Mr. Earnshaw?” I did not much like the thought of deliberately locking myself in with Heathcliff.

“Look at this!” he replied, pulling from his waistcoat an oddly made pistol with a double-edged spring knife attached to its barrel. “Quite a temptation for a desperate man, isn't it? Every night I can't resist taking this upstairs and trying his door. If I ever find it open, he's finished. I do it without fail, even if I've just thought of a hundred reasons why I shouldn't. Some devil urges me to ruin my own plans by killing him. You fight that devil for love's sake as long as you can. When the time comes, all the angels in heaven won't save him!”

I examined the weapon with curiosity. A dreadful thought struck me: what power I would have if I possessed such a thing! I took it from his hand and touched the blade. For one brief instant an expression crossed my face that astonished him. It wasn't horror; it was longing to own it. Jealously, he snatched the pistol back, folded the knife, and hid it again.
“I don't care if you tell him,” he said. “Warn him, and keep watch for him. I see you know how things stand between us. His danger doesn't shock you.”
“What has Heathcliff done to you?” I asked. “How has he injured you to deserve such terrible hatred? Wouldn't it be wiser to tell him to leave the house?”

“No!” Earnshaw thundered. “If he tries to leave me, he's a dead man. Persuade him to try it, and you'll be a murderess! Am I to lose _everything_ without a chance to win it back? Is Hareton to become a beggar? Oh, damn it! I _will_ get it back, and I'll have _his_ gold as well, and then his blood, and hell can have his soul! With that guest it will be ten times blacker than it ever was before!”

You've told me about your old master's habits, Ellen. He is plainly on the edge of madness; at least he was last night. I shuddered to be near him and thought the servant's ill-mannered sullenness almost pleasant by comparison. He began his gloomy pacing again. I lifted the latch and escaped into the kitchen. Joseph was bent over the fire, peering into a large pan suspended above it. A wooden bowl of oatmeal stood on the bench nearby. When the pan began to boil he turned to dip his hand into the bowl. I guessed he was making our supper, and, being hungry, determined that it should be fit to eat. “_I'll_ make the porridge!” I said sharply, moving the bowl out of his reach and beginning to take off my hat and riding clothes. “Mr. Earnshaw tells me to look after myself,” I continued, “and I will. I won't play the lady among you and risk starving.”

“Good Lord!” he muttered, sitting down and rubbing his ribbed stockings from knee to ankle. “If there's to be fresh orders—just when I've got used to two masters! If I mun have a _mistress_ over my head as well, it's time I were leaving. I never _did_ think I'd see t' day when I'd have to leave t' old place—but I reckon it's close at hand!”

I took no notice of his lament. I set briskly to work, sighing at the memory of a time when this would all have been a merry game, but soon forced to drive the memory away. Remembering past happiness was torture. The more danger there was of its ghost rising before me, the faster I stirred with the wooden stick and threw handfuls of oatmeal into the water. Joseph watched my cooking with increasing outrage.

“There!” he exclaimed. “Hareton, thou won't be eating thy porridge tonight. It'll be nowt but lumps as big as my fist. There, again! I'd throw t' bowl in an' all, if I were thee! There, tip t' slop out, and have done wi' it. Bang, bang. It's a mercy ye haven't knocked t' bottom out!”

I admit it _was_ rather a lumpy mess when I poured it into the bowls. Four bowls had been set out, and a gallon jug of fresh milk was brought from the dairy. Hareton seized the jug and began drinking from its broad lip, spilling as he went. I protested and asked that he should have his milk in a mug, saying I couldn't drink it after it had been treated so dirtily. The sour old man took enormous offence at my fastidiousness. He assured me over and over that “t' bairn's every bit as good as thee, and every bit as clean,” and wondered how I could manage to be so stuck-up. Meanwhile the little brute kept drinking and slobbering into the jug, glaring up at me in defiance.
“I'll have my supper in another room,” I said. “Isn't there somewhere you call a parlour?”
“_Parlour_!” he echoed with a sneer. “_Parlour_! Nay, we've no _parlours_. If ye don't like our company, there's master's; and if ye don't like master, there's us.”
“Then I'll go upstairs,” I answered. “Show me a room.”

I put my bowl on a tray and went to fetch fresh milk myself. Grumbling loudly, the man got up and led me upstairs. We climbed to the attics, and now and then he opened a door to peer into a room as we passed.

“Here's a room,” he said at last, flinging back a crooked board on hinges. “Good enough to eat a bit o' porridge in. There's a sack o' grain in t' corner, fairly clean. If ye're afraid o' dirtying those grand silk clothes, spread thy handkerchief over it.”
The “room” was a kind of storeroom that smelled strongly of malt and grain. Sacks were piled all round it, with a broad, bare space left in the middle.
“Why, man,” I cried, turning on him angrily, “this is no place to sleep. I want to see my bedroom.”
“_Bedroom_!” he repeated mockingly. “Ye shall see all t' _bedrooms_ there are. That one's mine.”
He pointed into the second attic, which differed from the first only in having barer walls and, at one end, a large, low bed without curtains, covered by an indigo quilt.
“What would I want with yours?” I snapped. “Surely Mr. Heathcliff doesn't sleep at the top of the house?”

“Oh! It's Master _Heathcliff's_ room ye're after?” he cried, as though the discovery were new. “Couldn't ye have said so straight off? Then I could've told ye, without all this bother, that's just t' one ye cannot see. He keeps it locked all t' time, and nobody meddles wi' it but himself.”

“You have a lovely house, Joseph,” I couldn't help remarking, “and such pleasant people in it. I think all the madness in the world must have gathered inside my head on the day I joined my fate to theirs! But that isn't the point just now. There are other rooms. For heaven's sake hurry, and let me settle somewhere!”

He did not answer my appeal, but trudged stubbornly down the wooden stairs and stopped at another room. From his stopping there, and the better furniture, I supposed it was the best bedroom. It had a good carpet, though dust hid the pattern; scraps of cut-paper decoration hung over the fireplace, falling to pieces; and there was a handsome oak bed with generous crimson curtains, fairly expensive and made in a modern style. But the curtains had clearly been roughly handled. The valances hung in loops, torn from their rings, and the iron rail was bent into a bow at one side, leaving the fabric trailing on the floor. The chairs were damaged too, many badly, and deep dents disfigured the wall panels. I was trying to summon the courage to enter and make myself at home when my fool of a guide announced, “This here's t' master's.” By then my supper was cold, my appetite gone, and my patience exhausted. I insisted on being given somewhere to take shelter and rest at once.

“Where t' devil—?” the pious old man began. “The Lord bless us! The Lord forgive us! Where t' _hell_ would ye go, ye spoiled, tiresome good-for-nowt! Ye've seen everywhere but Hareton's little room. There's not another hole to lie down in throughout t' house!”
I was so angry that I threw my tray and everything on it to the floor. Then I sat at the top of the stairs, buried my face in my hands, and cried.

“Eh! Eh!” Joseph exclaimed. “Well done, Miss Cathy! Well done, Miss Cathy! Now master'll trip over those broken pots, and then we'll hear summat. We'll hear what's to come of it. Good-for-nowt mad thing! Ye deserve to starve from now till Christmas, trampling God's precious gifts underfoot in thy terrible rages! But I'll be mistaken if ye keep that spirit long. Think Heathcliff will put up wi' such bonny ways? I only wish he'd catch thee at those tricks. I only wish he would.”

He went on scolding as he descended to his den below, taking the candle and leaving me in darkness. Thinking over my foolish outburst, I had to admit that I must swallow my pride, choke down my anger, and get up to clear away what I had done. Help arrived unexpectedly in the form of Throttler. I now recognised him as a son of our old Skulker: he had lived at the Grange as a puppy until my father gave him to Mr. Hindley. I think he knew me. He pressed his nose against mine in greeting, then hurried to devour the porridge while I felt my way from step to step, picking up broken crockery and wiping milk from the banister with my handkerchief. We had hardly finished when I heard Earnshaw in the passage. My helper tucked his tail between his legs and pressed against the wall; I slipped through the nearest doorway. The dog failed to escape him, judging by the scramble down the stairs and the long, pitiful yelping that followed. I was luckier. Earnshaw went past, entered his room, and shut the door. Immediately afterwards Joseph came up to put Hareton to bed. I had hidden in Hareton's room. Seeing me, the old man said, “I reckon there's room downstairs for both thee and thy pride now. It's empty. Ye can have it all to thyself—and Him who always makes a third in such wicked company!”

I gladly took the hint. The moment I dropped into a chair beside the fire, my head nodded and I fell asleep. I slept deeply and peacefully, though for far too short a time. Mr. Heathcliff woke me. He had just come in and demanded, in his loving way, what I was doing there. I explained why I was up so late: he had the key to our room in his pocket. The word _our_ gave mortal offence. He swore it wasn't mine and never would be, and that he would—but I won't repeat his words or describe how he habitually behaves. He is inventive and tireless in his efforts to make me loathe him! Sometimes I wonder at him so intensely that my fear grows numb. Yet I assure you, neither a tiger nor a poisonous snake could terrify me as he does. He told me about Catherine's illness and blamed my brother for causing it. Until he could get hold of Edgar, he promised, I would suffer in Edgar's place.
I hate him—I am miserable—I have been a fool! Don't breathe a word of this to anyone at the Grange. I shall look for you every day. Don't disappoint me!—ISABELLA.

chapters.title: Chapter XIV
paragraphs: As soon as I had read the letter, I went to the master. I told him that his sister had arrived at the Heights and had written to express her sorrow at Mrs. Linton's illness and her intense wish to see him. She hoped he would send her some sign of forgiveness through me as soon as possible.

“Forgiveness!” Linton said. “I have nothing to forgive her for, Ellen. You may go to Wuthering Heights this afternoon if you like. Tell her I'm not _angry_, but _sad_ to have lost her, especially as I cannot believe she will ever be happy. But visiting her is out of the question. We are separated for ever. If she truly wants to please me, let her persuade the villain she has married to leave the country.”
“Won't you write her just a little note, sir?” I asked pleadingly.
“No,” he answered. “There's no need. I shall have as little contact with Heathcliff's family as he has with mine. None at all!”

Mr. Edgar's coldness made me deeply unhappy. All the way from the Grange, I tried to think how I could put more warmth into his words when I repeated them, and soften his refusal to write even a few comforting lines to Isabella. I imagine she had been watching for me since morning. As I came up the paved garden path I saw her at the window and nodded, but she drew back as though afraid of being seen. I went in without knocking. Never had I seen such a dreary, miserable sight as that once cheerful house! I confess that, in the young lady's place, I would at least have swept the hearth and wiped the tables. But she had already caught the general spirit of neglect around her. Her pretty face was pale and lifeless, and her hair had not been curled: some strands hung straight down, while others were carelessly twisted round her head. She probably hadn't touched her clothes since the previous evening. Hindley was absent. Mr. Heathcliff sat at a table looking through papers in his pocketbook. When I appeared he got up, greeted me quite pleasantly, and offered me a chair. He was the only decent-looking thing in the room, and I thought I had never seen him look better. Circumstances had so reversed their positions that a stranger would certainly have taken him for a gentleman born and bred, and his wife for a thoroughly slovenly little creature! She hurried to greet me, holding out one hand for the letter she expected. I shook my head. She refused to understand, followed me to the sideboard where I put my bonnet, and whispered urgently that I must give her what I had brought. Heathcliff guessed what she was doing. “If you've brought anything for Isabella—and no doubt you have, Nelly—give it to her,” he said. “There's no need for secrecy. We have no secrets from each other.”

“Oh, I haven't brought anything,” I answered, deciding it was best to tell the truth at once. “My master asked me to tell his sister that she must expect neither a letter nor a visit from him for the present. He sends his love, ma'am, and his hopes for your happiness, and forgives you for the pain you've caused him. But he thinks that from now on the two households should have no contact, since nothing can come of keeping it up.”

Mrs. Heathcliff's lip trembled a little, and she went back to her seat by the window. Her husband stood near me on the hearth and began asking about Catherine. I told him as much about her illness as I thought proper, and his insistent questioning dragged out most of the facts about how it began. I blamed her, as she deserved, for bringing it on herself. I ended by saying I hoped he would follow Mr. Linton's example and stop interfering with the family, whether for good or ill.

“Mrs. Linton is only just recovering,” I said. “She'll never be what she was, but her life has been spared. If you really care for her, you'll keep out of her way—more than that, you'll leave this part of the country altogether. And so that you won't regret going, I'll tell you that Catherine Linton is now as different from your old friend Catherine Earnshaw as that young lady is from me. Her looks have changed greatly, and her character still more. Whoever is obliged to share her life will only be able to keep loving her through memories of what she once was, through ordinary human kindness, and through a sense of duty!”

“Quite possible,” Heathcliff said, forcing himself to appear calm. “Quite possible that your master has nothing left but ordinary human kindness and a sense of duty. But do you think I'll leave Catherine to his _duty_ and _kindness_? Can you compare what I feel for her with what he feels? Before you leave this house, you must promise to arrange a meeting for me with her. Whether you agree or refuse, I _will_ see her! What do you say?”
“I say, Mr. Heathcliff, that you mustn't,” I answered. “And you'll never do it through me. Another clash between you and the master would kill her outright.”

“With your help we can avoid that,” he continued. “And if there were any danger of such a clash—if he caused her one more moment of trouble—well, I think I would be justified in going to extremes! I wish you were honest enough to tell me whether Catherine would suffer greatly if she lost him. The fear that she would is what holds me back. There's the difference between our feelings. If he had been in my place and I in his, even if my hatred of him had poisoned my whole life, I would never have lifted a hand against him. Look as unbelieving as you please! I would never have driven him out of her company while she wanted him there. The moment she stopped caring for him, I would have torn out his heart and drunk his blood! But until then—if you don't believe me, you don't know me—until then, I would have died inch by inch before touching a hair on his head!”

“And yet,” I interrupted, “you feel no hesitation about destroying every hope of her full recovery. Just when she has almost forgotten you, you mean to force yourself back into her thoughts and plunge her into another storm of quarrelling and misery.”

“You think she's almost forgotten me?” he said. “Oh, Nelly! You know she hasn't! You know as well as I do that for every thought she gives Linton she gives a thousand to me! At the most miserable time of my life I did think something like that. It haunted me when I came back here last summer. But nothing except hearing it from her own lips could make me believe that dreadful idea again. And then Linton would mean nothing, nor Hindley, nor any dream I've ever had. My future would come down to two words: _death_ and _hell_. Living after losing her would be hell. Yet I was a fool to imagine for a moment that Edgar Linton's love meant more to her than mine. If he loved her with every power of his feeble little being, he couldn't love as much in eighty years as I could in one day. And Catherine's heart is as deep as mine. You could fit the sea into that horse trough as easily as he could claim all her love. Nonsense! He's hardly more precious to her than her dog or her horse. He hasn't it in him to be loved as I am. How can she love something in him that he doesn't possess?”
“Catherine and Edgar love each other as much as any two people can,” Isabella cried, suddenly roused. “Nobody has the right to speak like that, and I won't sit quietly while you belittle my brother!”
“Your brother is wonderfully fond of you too, isn't he?” Heathcliff remarked scornfully. “He's been surprisingly quick to turn you loose in the world.”
“He doesn't know what I'm suffering,” she answered. “I didn't tell him.”
“So you have told him something? You've written to him, have you?”
“I wrote to say I was married. You saw the note.”
“And you've written nothing since?”
“No, nothing.”
“My young lady looks sadly the worse for being married,” I observed. “Clearly someone's love has failed her. I can guess whose, though perhaps I'd better not say.”

“I'd guess it's her own,” said Heathcliff. “She's turning into a complete sloven! She's given up trying to please me remarkably soon. You'd hardly believe it, but the very day after our wedding she was crying to go home. Still, being less particular will make her fit into this house all the better. And I'll see that she doesn't disgrace me by wandering outside.”

“Well, sir,” I replied, “I hope you'll remember that Mrs. Heathcliff is used to being cared for and waited on. She was brought up as an only daughter, with everyone ready to serve her. You must give her a maid to keep things tidy for her, and you must treat her kindly. Whatever you think of Mr. Edgar, you cannot doubt that she is capable of deep affection. Otherwise she would never have given up the elegance, comforts, and friends of her old home to settle happily with you in a wilderness like this.”

“She gave them up under a delusion,” he answered. “She pictured me as the hero of a romance, whose chivalrous devotion would grant her every whim. I can hardly think of her as a rational creature: she was so stubborn about inventing a fanciful version of my character and acting on the false notions she treasured. But at last I think she's beginning to know me. I no longer see the foolish smiles and grimaces that first irritated me, or that senseless inability to understand that I meant what I said about her infatuation and about her. It was a marvellous feat of insight when she discovered that I didn't love her. At one point I thought no lesson would ever teach her that! Even now she hasn't learnt it properly. This morning she informed me, as though announcing something appalling, that I'd actually succeeded in making her hate me! A labour worthy of Hercules, I assure you! If I've managed it, I have reason to give thanks. Can I believe you, Isabella? Are you certain you hate me? If I leave you alone for half a day, won't you come sighing and coaxing me again? I expect she'd rather I had shown nothing but tenderness in front of you. Having the truth exposed hurts her vanity. But I don't care who knows that the passion was entirely on one side, and I never lied to her about it. She can't accuse me of showing the least false tenderness. The first thing she saw me do when we left the Grange was hang her little dog. When she begged for its life, my first words were that I wished I could hang every creature belonging to her, except one. Perhaps she imagined she was the exception. Yet no cruelty disgusted her. I suppose she naturally admires it, provided her own precious person is safe from harm! Wasn't it utterly absurd—sheer idiocy—for that pitiful, grovelling, mean-spirited bitch to dream that I could love her? Tell your master, Nelly, that I've never met anything so abject in my life. She even disgraces the name of Linton. Sometimes I've stopped experimenting on how much she can bear before she comes crawling shamefully back, simply because I've run out of ideas! But tell him this too, to reassure both the brother and the magistrate in him: I keep strictly within the law. So far I've carefully avoided giving her the slightest legal grounds for a separation. What's more, she wouldn't thank anyone for parting us. She could go if she wanted. The nuisance of having her here is greater than the pleasure of tormenting her!”

“Mr. Heathcliff,” I said, “you talk like a madman. Your wife probably believes you are mad, and that's why she has endured you until now. But since you say she may leave, I'm sure she'll take the opportunity. You're not so bewitched, ma'am, that you'd stay with him of your own free will?”

“Be careful, Ellen!” Isabella answered, her eyes blazing with anger. Their expression left no doubt that her husband had fully succeeded in making her detest him. “Don't believe a single word he says. He's a lying devil! A monster, not a human being! He's told me before that I could leave, and I tried, but I daren't try again! Only promise, Ellen, that you won't repeat a syllable of his vile talk to my brother or Catherine. Whatever he pretends, he wants to drive Edgar to desperation. He says he married me to gain power over him, and he shan't have it. I'll die first! I only hope, I pray, that he'll forget his devilish caution and kill me! The only happiness I can imagine is dying myself or seeing him dead!”

“There, that's enough for now!” Heathcliff said. “If you're called to give evidence in court, Nelly, remember her words! And look carefully at her face: she's almost reached the state that would suit me. No, Isabella, you're no longer fit to look after yourself. As your legal protector, I must keep you in my custody, however unpleasant that duty may be. Go upstairs. I want a private word with Ellen Dean. That's not the way. Upstairs, I said! Why, child, this is the way upstairs!”

He grabbed her and pushed her out of the room. When he came back he was muttering, “I have no pity! None! The more the worms wriggle, the more I want to crush their guts out! It's like teething in the soul: the worse the pain gets, the harder I grind.”
“Do you even understand the word pity?” I asked, hurrying to put on my bonnet. “Have you ever felt a trace of it in your life?”

“Put that down!” he interrupted, seeing that I meant to leave. “You're not going yet. Come here, Nelly. I must either persuade you or force you to help me see Catherine, and without delay. I swear I mean no harm. I don't want to cause a disturbance, or anger or insult Mr. Linton. I only want to hear from her own lips how she is and why she's been ill, and ask whether there's anything I can do for her. I spent six hours in the Grange garden last night, and I'll be back tonight. I'll haunt the place every night and every day until I find a way inside. If Edgar Linton comes across me, I won't hesitate to knock him down and give him enough to keep him quiet while I'm there. If his servants try to stop me, I'll frighten them off with these pistols. But wouldn't it be better to prevent me from meeting either them or their master? You could manage it so easily. I'd let you know when I arrived; then, as soon as she was alone, you could admit me without anyone seeing and keep watch until I left. Your conscience could be perfectly clear: you'd be preventing trouble.”

I protested that I would not betray my employer in his own house. I also insisted on the cruelty and selfishness of disturbing Mrs. Linton's peace merely to satisfy himself. “The most ordinary things give her a painful shock,” I said. “Her nerves are shattered, and I'm certain she couldn't bear the surprise. Don't insist, sir! If you do, I'll have to tell my master what you're planning, and he'll take steps to protect his house and everyone in it from such an outrageous intrusion!”

“In that case I'll take steps to keep you here, woman!” Heathcliff exclaimed. “You won't leave Wuthering Heights until tomorrow morning. It's ridiculous to claim that Catherine couldn't bear to see me. And I don't want to surprise her. You must prepare her—ask her whether I may come. You say she never mentions my name and nobody mentions me to her. Who could she speak to about me if I'm a forbidden subject in the house? She thinks you're all spying for her husband. Oh, I've no doubt she's in hell among you! Her silence tells me as much as anything else how she feels. You say she often looks restless and anxious. Is that proof she's at peace? You talk about her disturbed mind. How the devil could it be anything else, shut away in that dreadful loneliness? With that insipid, worthless creature nursing her out of _duty_ and _human kindness_! Out of _pity_ and _charity_! He might as well plant an oak in a flowerpot and expect it to flourish as think she can grow strong again in the shallow soil of his concerns! We'll settle this now. Will you stay here while I fight my way past Linton and his servant to Catherine? Or will you be my friend, as you always have been, and do what I ask? Decide! If you insist on being stubborn and spiteful, there's no reason for me to wait another minute!”

Well, Mr. Lockwood, I argued, complained, and refused him outright fifty times, but in the end he forced me to agree. I undertook to carry a letter to my mistress. If she consented, I promised to tell him when Linton would next be away, so he could come and get inside as best he could. I wouldn't be there, and the other servants would also be out of the way. Was that right or wrong? I'm afraid it was wrong, though it seemed practical. I thought that giving in would prevent another explosion. I also thought it might bring a helpful turning point in Catherine's mental illness. Then I remembered Mr. Edgar's stern rebuke for carrying tales. I tried to soothe my misgivings by assuring myself again and again that this betrayal of trust—if it deserved such a harsh name—would be my last. Even so, my walk home was sadder than my journey there, and I had many doubts before I could bring myself to place the letter in Mrs. Linton's hand.
But Kenneth is here. I'll go down and tell him how much better you are. My story is _dree_, as we say—long and drawn out—and will help pass another morning.

Dree, and dreary! I thought, as the good woman went downstairs to meet the doctor. Hardly the sort of entertainment I would have chosen, either. But never mind! I'll make wholesome medicine from Mrs. Dean's bitter herbs. First of all, I must guard against the fascination in Catherine Heathcliff's shining eyes. I would be in a pretty predicament if I gave my heart to that young woman and the daughter proved to be another version of her mother.

chapters.title: Chapter XV
paragraphs: Another week has passed, bringing me that much closer to health and spring! By now I have heard my neighbour's whole history, in several sittings whenever the housekeeper could spare time from more important work. I shall continue in her own words, shortening them only a little. On the whole she tells a story very well, and I doubt I could improve her style.

That evening, she said—the evening after my visit to the Heights—I knew as certainly as if I had seen him that Mr. Heathcliff was somewhere outside. I avoided going out because his letter was still in my pocket and I wanted no more threats or pestering. I had decided to wait until my master went out before giving it to Catherine, as I could not predict how she would react. As a result, three days passed before she received it. The fourth day was Sunday. Once the family had left for church, I took it to her room. One manservant had stayed behind to look after the house with me. We generally locked the doors during the service, but the weather was so warm and pleasant that I left them wide open. Knowing who was coming, I then kept my promise by telling the man that our mistress badly wanted oranges. He must run to the village for a few, I said, and we would pay for them tomorrow. He went off, and I went upstairs.

Mrs. Linton was sitting as usual in the open window recess, wearing a loose white dress with a light shawl round her shoulders. Some of her long, thick hair had been cut off when she first fell ill. Now it was simply combed into its natural waves over her temples and neck. Her appearance had changed, as I had told Heathcliff, but when she was calm the change gave her an almost unearthly beauty. The fire in her eyes had become a dreamy, sorrowful softness. They no longer seemed to look at the things around her, but always beyond them—far beyond, as though outside this world. Her face was still pale, though it had lost its wasted look as she regained weight. That pallor, and the strange expression caused by her state of mind, painfully recalled their causes and made her still more moving to look at. To me, certainly—and, I should think, to anyone who saw her—they contradicted the clearer signs of recovery and marked her as someone doomed to fade away.

An open book lay on the windowsill in front of her, its pages stirred now and then by the faintest breeze. I think Linton had put it there. She never tried to distract herself by reading or by doing anything else, and he would spend hours trying to interest her in something she had once enjoyed. She knew what he was attempting. In her better moods she patiently allowed it, betraying its failure only by an occasional half-suppressed sigh of weariness, until at last she stopped him with the saddest of smiles and kisses. At other times she turned away irritably and hid her face in her hands, or even pushed him off in anger. Then he was careful to leave her alone, knowing that he could do no good.

The bells of Gimmerton chapel were still ringing. From the valley came the soothing sound of the stream, full and softly flowing. It was a lovely substitute for the rustle of summer leaves, not yet heard; when the trees were in leaf, they drowned out that music round the Grange. At Wuthering Heights you could always hear the stream on still days after a great thaw or a spell of steady rain. And Catherine was thinking of Wuthering Heights as she listened—if she was thinking or listening at all. She had that vague, faraway look I mentioned, which showed no awareness of the physical world, either through sight or sound.

“Here's a letter for you, Mrs. Linton,” I said, gently placing it in the hand resting on her knee. “You must read it now, because it needs an answer. Shall I break the seal?” “Yes,” she answered, without moving her eyes. I opened it; it was very short. “Now read it,” I went on. She pulled her hand away and let the letter drop. I put it back in her lap and stood waiting for her to look down. After such a long wait that I lost patience, I spoke again. “Shall I read it to you, ma'am? It's from Mr. Heathcliff.”

She started. A troubled flash of recognition crossed her face, followed by a struggle to gather her thoughts. She picked up the letter and appeared to read it, sighing when she reached the signature. But I could see she had still not understood its meaning: when I asked for her answer, she simply pointed to the name and looked at me with sorrowful, eager questioning.
“He wants to see you,” I explained, realising that she needed help to understand. “He'll be in the garden by now, impatient to hear what answer I bring.”

As I spoke, I saw a large dog lying on the sunny grass below prick up its ears as though about to bark, then lay them back and wag its tail: whoever was approaching was someone it knew. Mrs. Linton leaned forward, listening breathlessly. A moment later footsteps crossed the hall. The open doors had been too tempting for Heathcliff to resist. He probably thought I meant to evade my promise and decided to rely on his own boldness. Catherine stared towards her bedroom doorway with desperate eagerness. He did not find the right room at once. She motioned for me to let him in, but before I reached the door he found it himself. In a stride or two he was beside her, holding her in his arms.

For about five minutes he neither spoke nor let her go. I daresay he gave her more kisses in that time than he had given in all his life before. But my mistress had kissed him first, and I could plainly see that sheer agony made it almost unbearable for him to look into her face! The moment he saw her, the same certainty had struck him as had struck me: there was no hope of a lasting recovery. Her fate was settled. She would die.

“Oh, Cathy! Oh, my life! How can I bear this?” were his first words, spoken with no attempt to hide his despair. He stared at her so intensely that I thought the force of his gaze alone must bring tears to his eyes. But they burned with anguish; they did not soften into tears.

“What is it now?” Catherine said. She leaned back and returned his gaze, her brow suddenly darkening: her mood swung like a weather vane with every changing impulse. “You and Edgar have broken my heart, Heathcliff! And now you both come to lament what you've done, as though you were the ones who deserved pity! Well, you'll get none from me. You've killed me, and it seems to have done you good. How strong you are! How many years do you mean to live after I'm gone?”
Heathcliff had gone down on one knee to hold her. He tried to get up, but she caught his hair and kept him there.

“I wish I could hold you here,” she went on bitterly, “until we were both dead! I wouldn't care how much you suffered. Your suffering means nothing to me. Why shouldn't you suffer? I do! Will you forget me? Will you be happy when I'm in the ground? Twenty years from now, will you say, ‘That's Catherine Earnshaw's grave. I loved her long ago and was miserable when I lost her, but it's over now. I've loved many others since. My children are dearer to me than she was, and when I die I won't be glad to go to her; I'll be sorry to leave them!’ Will you say that, Heathcliff?”
“Don't torment me until I'm as mad as you are,” he cried, wrenching his head free and grinding his teeth.

To anyone watching calmly, the two of them would have made a strange and frightening picture. No wonder Catherine thought heaven would be a place of exile unless she left her character behind along with her mortal body. A wild desire for revenge showed in her white cheeks, bloodless lips, and glittering eyes. Her clenched fingers still held some of the hair she had seized. Meanwhile her companion had caught her arm with one hand as he pushed himself up with the other. He had so little of the gentleness her condition required that, when he let go, I saw four distinct blue marks on her colourless skin.

“Has a devil got into you,” he went on savagely, “that you can talk to me like this when you're dying? Don't you realise every word will be burnt into my memory, eating deeper for ever after you've left me? You know you're lying when you say I've killed you. And you know, Catherine, that I could forget my own existence as easily as I could forget you! Isn't it enough for your hellish selfishness that you'll be at peace while I writhe in the tortures of hell?”

“I won't be at peace,” Catherine moaned. Her heart was beating so violently and unevenly from all this agitation that its movements could be seen and heard, bringing home to her how weak she was. She said nothing until the attack passed. Then she went on more gently:

“I don't wish you any more suffering than I have myself, Heathcliff. I only wish that we should never be separated. If anything I've said hurts you afterwards, remember that I'll feel the same hurt underground, and forgive me for my own sake! Come here and kneel beside me again! You've never harmed me in your life. No, if you stay angry, that will be worse to remember than my cruel words! Won't you come back here? Please!”

Heathcliff went behind her chair and leaned over it, but not far enough for her to see his face, which was ashen with emotion. She twisted round to look at him. He would not allow it. Turning abruptly, he walked to the fireplace and stood silently with his back to us. Mrs. Linton watched him suspiciously; every movement stirred a new feeling in her. After a pause and a long stare, she spoke again, turning to me with wounded indignation in her voice:

“Oh, you see, Nelly, he wouldn't soften for a moment, even to keep me out of the grave. _That's_ how much I'm loved! Well, never mind. That isn't _my_ Heathcliff. I'll go on loving mine and take him with me. He's in my soul. And,” she added thoughtfully, “what troubles me most, after all, is this broken prison. I'm tired of being shut inside it. I'm longing to escape into that glorious world and stay there for ever, instead of seeing it dimly through tears and yearning for it through the walls of an aching heart. I want to be truly with it, inside it. Nelly, you think yourself better off and luckier than me, with all your health and strength. You pity me. Very soon that will change. I'll be the one pitying _you_. I'll be so far beyond and above you all that there will be no comparison. I _wonder_ why he won't come near me!” she continued to herself. “I thought he wanted to. Heathcliff, dear! This is no time to sulk. Please come to me, Heathcliff.”

In her eagerness she got up, supporting herself on the arm of the chair. At that heartfelt plea he turned, looking utterly desperate. His eyes, wide and at last wet with tears, flashed fiercely at her; his chest heaved uncontrollably. For an instant they stayed apart. Then I scarcely saw how they came together: Catherine sprang forward, he caught her, and they clung to each other so tightly that I thought my mistress would never come out of his embrace alive. Indeed, she seemed to lose consciousness at once. He dropped into the nearest chair. When I hurried over to see whether she had fainted, he bared his teeth at me and foamed like a mad dog, clutching her jealously to him. I felt that I was facing something other than a creature of my own kind. He seemed beyond understanding anything I might say, so I stood back, silent and deeply bewildered.
Presently Catherine moved, which eased my fears a little. She raised her hand to clasp his neck and draw his cheek to hers as he held her. Covering her with frantic caresses, he said wildly:

“Now you're showing me how cruel you've been—cruel and faithless. _Why_ did you scorn me? _Why_ did you betray your own heart, Cathy? I have no comfort to offer you. You deserve this. You've killed yourself. Yes, kiss me and cry; force kisses and tears out of me. They'll wither you; they'll damn you. You loved me—what _right_ did you have to leave me, then? What right—answer me—for that paltry fancy you felt for Linton? Misery, humiliation, death, nothing God or Satan could inflict would have parted us. Yet _you_ did it willingly. I haven't broken your heart. _You_ have broken it, and in breaking yours you've broken mine. It's all the worse for me that I'm strong. Do I want to live? What kind of life will it be when you—oh, God! Would _you_ want to live with your soul in the grave?”
“Leave me alone. Leave me alone,” Catherine sobbed. “If I've done wrong, I'm dying for it. Isn't that enough! You left me too, but I won't reproach you! I forgive you. Forgive me!”

“It's hard to forgive while I look into those eyes and feel those wasted hands,” he answered. “Kiss me again, and don't let me see your eyes! I forgive what you've done to me. I love _my_ murderer—but _yours_! How can I?”

They fell silent, hiding their faces against each other, their cheeks wet with each other's tears. At least I suppose both of them were crying: it appeared Heathcliff _could_ weep on an occasion as great as this.

Meanwhile I grew increasingly uneasy. The afternoon was slipping away, the servant I had sent out returned with his purchases, and in the western sunlight shining up the valley I could see a crowd gathering outside the porch of Gimmerton chapel.
“The service has finished,” I announced. “My master will be home in half an hour.”
