Heathcliff groaned out a curse and clasped Catherine tighter. She did not stir.

Soon I saw a group of servants coming up the road towards the kitchen wing. Mr. Linton followed not far behind. He opened the gate himself and walked slowly up, probably enjoying the beautiful afternoon, as soft and warm as summer.
“He's here now!” I cried. “For heaven's sake, hurry downstairs! There's nobody on the front staircase. Be quick, and stay among the trees until he's safely inside.”
“I have to go, Cathy,” Heathcliff said, trying to free himself from her arms. “But if I'm alive, I'll see you again before you sleep. I won't go five yards from your window.”
“You mustn't leave!” she answered, holding him with all the strength she had. “I tell you, you _shall_ not.”
“Just for one hour,” he pleaded urgently.
“Not even one minute,” she answered.
“I _have_ to—Linton will be upstairs any moment,” the frightened intruder insisted.
He tried to rise, which would have loosened her fingers. She clung to him, gasping, with a look of wild determination.
“No!” she screamed. “Oh, don't, don't leave me. This is the last time! Edgar won't hurt us. Heathcliff, I'll die! I'll die!”
“Damn the fool! There he is,” Heathcliff cried, sinking back into the chair. “Hush, my darling! Hush, hush, Catherine! I'll stay. If he shot me like this, I'd die blessing him.”
So there they were, locked together again. I heard my master coming up the stairs. Cold sweat ran down my forehead; I was terrified.

“Are you really going to listen to her ravings?” I said furiously. “She doesn't know what she's saying. Will you destroy her because she hasn't the sense to save herself? Get up! You could free yourself in a moment. This is the most devilish thing you've ever done. We're all ruined—master, mistress, and servant.”
I wrung my hands and cried out, and the noise made Mr. Linton quicken his step. Even in my distress, I was honestly glad to see Catherine's arms drop slackly and her head fall forward.
“She's fainted, or she's dead,” I thought. “So much the better. Far better for her to die than linger on as a burden, making everyone round her miserable.”

Edgar rushed towards his uninvited guest, white with astonishment and rage. I cannot say what he intended to do. But Heathcliff stopped any action at once by placing the seemingly lifeless body in his arms.
“Look at her!” he said. “Unless you're a devil, help her first. You can speak to me afterwards!”

He went into the parlour and sat down. Mr. Linton called me, and after great difficulty and many attempts we managed to bring Catherine round. But she was completely confused. She sighed and moaned and recognised no one. In his anxiety for her, Edgar forgot the friend he hated. I did not. At the first opportunity I went to Heathcliff and begged him to leave, assuring him that Catherine was better and promising to tell him in the morning how she had passed the night.

“I won't refuse to go outside,” he answered, “but I'll stay in the garden. And Nelly, be sure you keep your word tomorrow. I'll be under those larch trees. Mind you do! Otherwise I'll pay another visit, whether Linton is here or not.”
He cast a quick look through the half-open bedroom door. Seeing that what I had said appeared to be true, he relieved the house of his ill-fated presence.

chapters.title: Chapter XVI
paragraphs: At about midnight, the Catherine you saw at Wuthering Heights was born: a frail baby, two months premature. Her mother died two hours later, never having regained enough awareness to miss Heathcliff or recognise Edgar. His grief at losing her is too painful a subject to dwell on. Its later effects showed how deeply it had wounded him. To my mind, it was made much worse by his being left without a male heir. Looking at the weak little orphan, I mourned that fact and inwardly blamed old Mr. Linton for settling his property on his own daughter rather than his son's daughter, though this was only a natural preference on his part. What an unwelcome baby she was, poor thing! In those first hours she might have cried herself out of existence without anyone caring in the least. We made up for that neglect later, but her beginning was as friendless as her end is likely to be.

The next morning was bright and cheerful outside. Its light filtered softly through the blinds of the silent room, bathing the bed and the figure on it in a gentle, tender glow. Edgar Linton lay with his head on the pillow and his eyes closed. His young, handsome face was almost as deathlike and motionless as the one beside him. But _his_ stillness came from exhausted grief, and _hers_ from perfect peace. Her forehead was smooth, her eyelids closed, and her lips seemed to smile. No angel in heaven could have looked more beautiful. I shared in the infinite calm around her. My mind has never felt more holy than while I looked at that undisturbed image of divine rest. Instinctively I echoed her words from a few hours earlier: “Beyond and above us all, beyond comparison! Whether still on earth or already in heaven, her spirit is at home with God!”

I don't know whether this is peculiar to me, but I am seldom anything other than happy when keeping watch in a room with the dead, provided no frantic or despairing mourner shares the task. I see a rest that neither earth nor hell can disturb. I feel certain of the endless, shadowless life beyond—the eternity they have entered, where life has no limit in its duration, love none in its sympathy, and joy none in its fullness. That day I noticed how much selfishness there was even in a love like Mr. Linton's, since he so bitterly regretted Catherine's blessed release! Certainly, after the wilful, impatient life she had led, one might have doubted whether she deserved a peaceful haven at last. One might doubt it in moments of cool reflection, but not there beside her body. Its very stillness declared its peace, and seemed to promise the same peace to the spirit that had lived in it.
Do you believe people like her _are_ happy in the next world, sir? I'd give a great deal to know.
I chose not to answer Mrs. Dean's question, which seemed to me a little unorthodox in its religious implications. She went on:
Looking back over Catherine Linton's life, I'm afraid we have no right to think she is. But we'll leave her to her Maker.

The master appeared to be asleep. Soon after sunrise I ventured to leave the room and slip outside into the fresh, reviving air. The servants thought I was shaking off the sleepiness of my long vigil, but my real purpose was to see Mr. Heathcliff. If he had stayed among the larches all night, he would have heard nothing of the activity at the Grange, except perhaps the messenger galloping to Gimmerton. If he had come closer, the lights moving back and forth and the doors opening and shutting would probably have told him that something was wrong. I both wanted and dreaded to find him. He had to be told the terrible news, and I longed to get it over with, but I had no idea _how_ to tell him. He was there, a few yards farther into the park, leaning against an old ash tree without his hat. His hair was soaked with dew that had collected on the budding branches and was pattering down around him. He must have stood like that a long time. A pair of blackbirds flew back and forth scarcely three feet away, busy building their nest and no more concerned by him than by a piece of wood. They flew off as I approached. He raised his eyes and spoke. “She's dead!” he said. “I didn't need to wait for you to know that. Put away your handkerchief. Don't snivel in front of me. Damn you all! She has no need of _your_ tears!”

I was crying as much for him as for her. Sometimes we pity creatures who feel no pity for themselves or anyone else. At my first look into his face I knew that he had learnt of the disaster. Because his lips were moving and his eyes were lowered to the ground, the foolish thought struck me that his heart had been humbled and that he was praying.
“Yes, she's dead!” I answered, holding back my sobs and wiping my cheeks. “Gone to heaven, I hope, where every one of us may join her if we heed the warning and turn from evil ways to good!”
“Did _she_ heed the warning, then?” Heathcliff asked, trying to sneer. “Did she die like a saint? Come, tell me exactly what happened. How did—?”

He tried to say her name but could not. Pressing his lips together, he fought silently against his inner agony, meeting my sympathy all the while with a fierce, unflinching stare. “How did she die?” he asked at last. For all his toughness, he was glad of the support behind him: after that struggle, he shook involuntarily to the tips of his fingers.

“Poor wretch!” I thought. “You have a heart and nerves like the rest of mankind! Why are you so anxious to hide them? Your pride can't blind God! You're tempting him to wring them until he forces you to cry out in humiliation.”
“As quietly as a lamb!” I said aloud. “She sighed and stretched, like a child half waking and then slipping back to sleep. Five minutes later I felt one faint beat at her heart, and then nothing!”
“And—did she mention me at all?” he asked hesitantly, as though afraid the answer would bring details he could not bear to hear.

“Her senses never came back. She recognised nobody after you left her,” I said. “She lies with a sweet smile on her face. Her last thoughts wandered back to the happy days of her childhood. Her life ended in a gentle dream. May her waking in the next world be as gentle!”

“May she wake in agony!” he cried with terrifying violence, stamping his foot and groaning as an uncontrollable storm of feeling seized him. “Why, she's a liar to the very end! Where is she? Not _there_, not in heaven, not destroyed—where? Oh! You said my suffering meant nothing to you! Then I have one prayer, and I'll repeat it until my tongue can no longer move: Catherine Earnshaw, may you never rest as long as I live! You said I killed you—then haunt me! The murdered _do_ haunt their murderers, I believe. I know ghosts _have_ walked the earth. Stay with me always, in any form you choose. Drive me mad! Only _don't_ leave me in this pit where I cannot find you! Oh, God! It cannot be spoken! I _cannot_ live without my life! I _cannot_ live without my soul!”

He struck his head against the knotted trunk, raised his eyes, and howled. It was not a man's cry, but that of a wild animal being tortured to death with knives and spears. I saw several splashes of blood on the bark; his hand and forehead were stained as well. What I was seeing had probably happened more than once during the night. It scarcely stirred pity in me: it horrified me. Still, I was reluctant to leave him like that. But as soon as he recovered enough to notice me watching, he thundered an order to go, and I obeyed. Calming or comforting him was beyond anything I could do!

Mrs. Linton's funeral was set for the Friday after her death. Until then her open coffin stood in the great drawing room, scattered with flowers and fragrant leaves. Linton watched over it day and night without sleeping. Heathcliff, as nobody but me knew, spent at least his nights outside, equally unable to rest. I did not speak to him, but I knew he meant to get in if he could. On Tuesday, a little after dark, my master was at last forced by exhaustion to lie down for a couple of hours. I went and opened one of the windows. Heathcliff's persistence had moved me to give him the chance of one last farewell to the faded form of the woman he worshipped. He took that chance, cautiously and briefly, without making the slightest sound to betray himself. Indeed, I would never have known he had come if the cloth around her face had not been disturbed, and if I had not seen a curl of fair hair on the floor, tied with silver thread. When I examined it, I found that it came from the locket round Catherine's neck. Heathcliff had opened the locket, thrown out its contents, and replaced them with a black lock of his own hair. I twisted the two locks together and put them both inside.

Mr. Earnshaw was naturally invited to accompany his sister's body to the grave. He offered no excuse, but never came. Apart from her husband, the mourners were all tenants and servants. Isabella received no invitation.

To the villagers' surprise, Catherine was buried neither inside the chapel beneath the Lintons' carved monument nor outside beside her own family's graves. Her grave was dug on a green slope in a corner of the churchyard, where the wall is so low that heather and bilberry plants have spread over it from the moor, and peat soil almost buries it. Her husband lies beside her now. Each grave has a simple headstone and a plain grey block at its foot.

chapters.title: Chapter XVII
paragraphs: That Friday was our last fine day for a month. The weather broke in the evening. The wind swung from south to northeast, bringing rain, then sleet and snow. By morning it was hard to believe we had enjoyed three weeks of summer. Primroses and crocuses lay buried under wintry drifts; the larks had fallen silent, and the first leaves on the early trees were struck black by the cold. What a dreary, bitter, miserable day followed! My master stayed in his room. I took over the deserted parlour and made it into a nursery. There I sat with the whimpering little doll of a baby on my lap, rocking her and watching the snowflakes pile up against the uncurtained window, when the door opened and someone came in, breathless and laughing! For a moment my anger outweighed my surprise. Assuming it was one of the maids, I cried, “Stop that! How dare you bring your silliness in here? What would Mr. Linton say if he heard you?”
“Forgive me!” a familiar voice answered. “But I know Edgar's in bed, and I can't help myself.”
The speaker came towards the fire, panting and pressing a hand to her side.

“I've run all the way from Wuthering Heights!” she continued after a moment. “Except where I flew. I couldn't count how many times I've fallen. Oh, I ache everywhere! Don't be frightened! I'll explain as soon as I can. Just be kind enough to go and order the carriage to take me on to Gimmerton, and ask a servant to find some clothes in my wardrobe.”

Our visitor was Mrs. Heathcliff. She certainly did not look as though she had anything to laugh about. Her hair hung over her shoulders, dripping with water and snow. She wore her usual girlish dress, more suited to her age than to her married position: a low-necked frock with short sleeves, and nothing covering either her head or her neck. Its thin silk clung to her, soaking wet, and only flimsy slippers protected her feet. Add a deep cut beneath one ear, kept from bleeding heavily only by the cold, a white face covered in scratches and bruises, and a body so exhausted it could scarcely stand, and you can imagine that examining her did little to ease my first alarm.

“My dear young lady,” I exclaimed, “I'm not going anywhere or listening to anything until you've taken off every stitch and put on dry clothes. And you certainly aren't going to Gimmerton tonight, so there's no point ordering the carriage.”
“I certainly am,” she said, “whether on foot or in the carriage. But I've no objection to being properly dressed. And—ah, look, it's running down my neck now! The fire makes it sting.”

She would not let me touch her until I had done as she asked. Only after the coachman had been told to get ready and a maid sent to pack the necessary clothes did she allow me to bandage her wound and help her change.

“Now, Ellen,” she said when I had finished and she was sitting in an easy chair by the fire, with a cup of tea before her, “sit opposite me and put poor Catherine's baby away. I don't like seeing it! Don't think I cared little for Catherine because I behaved so foolishly when I came in. I've cried too, bitterly—yes, and with more reason than anyone else. You remember we parted without making peace, and I shall never forgive myself. But even so, I wasn't going to sympathise with him, the brute! Oh, give me the poker! This is the last thing of his I still have.” She slipped the gold ring from her finger and threw it on the floor. “I'll smash it!” she went on, striking at it with childish malice. “Then I'll burn it!” She picked up the battered thing and dropped it among the coals. “There! If he ever gets me back, he'll have to buy another. He's quite capable of coming after me just to torment Edgar. I daren't stay in case that idea enters his wicked head! Besides, Edgar hasn't been kind, has he? I won't come begging for his help, and I won't bring him more trouble. I had to take shelter here. But if I hadn't heard he was out of the way, I would have stopped in the kitchen, washed my face, warmed myself, had you fetch what I needed, and gone again—anywhere beyond the reach of my cursed—of that living goblin! Ah, he was in such a rage! If he'd caught me! What a pity Earnshaw isn't as strong as he is. If Hindley could have done it, I wouldn't have run until I'd seen him almost beaten to pieces!”

“Now, don't talk so fast, Miss!” I interrupted. “You'll loosen the handkerchief I've tied round your face and start the cut bleeding again. Drink your tea, get your breath, and stop laughing. Laughter is sadly out of place in this house, and in your condition!”
“That's certainly true,” she replied. “Listen to that child! It never stops wailing. Send it somewhere I can't hear it for an hour. I shan't stay longer than that.”
I rang the bell and gave the baby into a servant's care. Then I asked what had driven her to flee Wuthering Heights in such a state, and where she intended to go, since she refused to stay with us.

“I ought to stay, and I wanted to,” she answered, “to comfort Edgar and look after the baby, for a start, and because the Grange is my rightful home. But I tell you, he wouldn't allow it! Do you think he could bear to see me healthy and happy, or think of us living peacefully, without deciding to poison our comfort? At least I have the satisfaction of knowing that he hates me so much it seriously annoys him to have me within sight or hearing. Whenever I come near him, I see his face twist involuntarily with hatred, partly because he knows how good a reason I have to hate him, and partly from his own natural dislike. It's strong enough to make me fairly certain he wouldn't chase me all over England, if I managed to get clean away. That's why I must leave altogether. I no longer want him to kill me. I'd rather he killed himself! He's thoroughly put out the love I felt for him, so that no longer troubles me. I can still remember how I loved him, and can faintly imagine I might love him yet if—no, no! Even if he had adored me, his devilish nature would have shown itself somehow. Catherine must have had terribly twisted tastes to care so much for him when she knew him so well. Monster! I wish he could be wiped out of existence and out of my memory!”
“Hush, hush! He's a human being,” I said. “Show a little more charity. There are worse men in the world!”

“He isn't a human being,” she retorted, “and he has no claim on my charity. I gave him my heart, and he squeezed the life out of it and threw it back at me. People feel with their hearts, Ellen. Since he's destroyed mine, I have nothing left to feel for him with. And I wouldn't, even if he groaned from now until his dying day and wept tears of blood for Catherine! No, indeed, indeed I wouldn't!” Here Isabella began to cry, but immediately brushed the tears from her lashes and went on. “You asked what finally drove me to run? I was forced to try because I'd managed to push his anger beyond his malice. Pulling out nerves with red-hot pincers takes more calmness than smashing a head. I worked him up until he forgot the devilish caution he was so proud of and became murderously violent. I enjoyed knowing that I could enrage him. That pleasure woke my instinct to save myself, so I broke free completely. If I ever fall into his hands again, he's welcome to take a spectacular revenge.

“Yesterday, as you know, Mr. Earnshaw ought to have attended the funeral. He kept sober for the occasion—fairly sober, that is: he didn't go raving to bed at six and get up drunk at twelve. Consequently he rose in such suicidal misery that he was no more fit for church than for a dance. Instead he sat by the fire, swallowing gin or brandy by the tumblerful.

“Heathcliff—I shudder at his name!—has hardly belonged to the household from last Sunday until today. Whether angels have fed him, or his relatives down below, I can't tell, but he hasn't eaten a meal with us for nearly a week. He has merely come home at dawn, gone upstairs, and locked himself in his room, as though anyone dreamed of wanting his company! There he has stayed, praying like a Methodist, except that the god he begged was unfeeling dust and ashes. When he addressed God, he seemed oddly to confuse him with his own dark father! Once these precious prayers were over—and they generally lasted until he grew hoarse and his voice choked in his throat—he went out again, always straight to the Grange! I'm surprised Edgar didn't send for a constable and have him arrested! For my part, though I grieved for Catherine, I couldn't help treating this release from degrading oppression as a holiday.

“My spirits recovered enough for me to hear Joseph's endless sermons without crying, and to walk about the house less like a frightened thief. You wouldn't think anything Joseph said could make me cry, but he and Hareton are hateful companions. I'd rather sit with Hindley and listen to his dreadful talk than with ‘t' little master’ and his faithful supporter, that odious old man! When Heathcliff is home, I'm often forced into the kitchen with them, unless I want to freeze in the damp, empty rooms. When he's away, as he has been this week, I put a table and chair in a corner by the main fire and leave Mr. Earnshaw to do as he pleases. He doesn't interfere with my arrangements. Unless someone provokes him, he's quieter than he used to be: more sullen and depressed, less furious. Joseph insists he's a changed man, that the Lord has touched his heart and he is saved ‘as if through fire’. I can't make out any signs of this happy improvement, but that's no concern of mine.

“Last night I sat in my corner reading old books until nearly twelve. The thought of going upstairs was so dismal, with the snowstorm outside and my mind constantly returning to the churchyard and the fresh grave! I hardly dared look up from the page, because that mournful scene instantly rose before me. Hindley sat opposite with his head on his hand, perhaps thinking of the same thing. He had stopped drinking before he lost his reason, and for two or three hours had neither moved nor spoken. The only sounds in the house were the moaning wind, which sometimes shook the windows, the faint crackle of coals, and the click of my candle snuffers as I trimmed the long wick now and then. Hareton and Joseph were probably fast asleep. It was very, very sad. As I read I sighed, feeling as though all happiness had gone from the world and would never return.

“At last the sound of the kitchen latch broke the gloomy silence. Heathcliff had come back from his vigil earlier than usual, probably because of the sudden storm. That door was fastened, and we heard him coming round to try the other. I got up, unable to keep my feelings from finding words. My companion, who had been staring towards the door, turned to look at me.
“‘I'll keep him out for five minutes,’ he exclaimed. ‘You won't object?’
“‘You can keep him out all night for all I care,’ I answered. ‘Do! Put the key in the lock and slide the bolts.’

“Earnshaw did it before his guest reached the front. Then he brought his chair to the other side of my table and leaned over, searching my eyes for a hatred that answered the burning hatred in his own. Since he looked and felt like a murderer, he did not quite find that. But he found enough to encourage him to speak.

“‘You and I,’ he said, ‘each have a great debt to settle with the man out there! If neither of us were a coward, we could join forces and repay it. Are you as soft as your brother? Will you endure everything to the bitter end without ever trying to strike back?’

“‘I'm tired of enduring it already,’ I replied. ‘I'd welcome revenge that wouldn't turn against me. But treachery and violence are spears with a point at each end. They wound the people who use them worse than their enemies.’

“‘Treachery and violence deserve treachery and violence in return!’ Hindley cried. ‘Mrs. Heathcliff, I ask you to do nothing but sit still and hold your tongue. Tell me, can you do that? I'm sure you'd enjoy seeing the fiend's life end as much as I would. He'll be the death of _you_ unless you outwit him, and the ruin of _me_. Damn the hellish villain! He's knocking as though he already owned the house! Promise to keep quiet, and before that clock strikes—it's three minutes to one—you'll be a free woman!’
“He took from his breast the weapon I described in my letter and was about to lower the candle flame. I snatched the candle away and caught his arm.
“‘I won't keep quiet!’ I said. ‘You mustn't touch him. Leave the door shut and sit still!’

“‘No! I've made up my mind, and by God I'll do it!’ the desperate man cried. ‘I'll do you a kindness whether you want it or not, and give Hareton justice! You needn't trouble to protect me. Catherine is gone. Nobody alive would grieve for me or feel ashamed if I cut my throat this minute. It's time to make an end!’
“I might as well have wrestled with a bear or tried to reason with a madman. All I could do was run to a window and warn his intended victim of what awaited him.
“‘You'd better find somewhere else to sleep tonight!’ I called, with a rather triumphant note. ‘Mr. Earnshaw means to shoot you if you keep trying to get in.’
“‘You'd better open the door, you—’ he answered, calling me some elegant name I don't choose to repeat.
“‘I won't interfere,’ I retorted. ‘Come in and get shot if you like. I've done my duty.’

“I shut the window and went back to the fire. I didn't have enough hypocrisy in me to pretend concern about the danger he was in. Earnshaw cursed me furiously, insisting I still loved the villain and calling me every sort of name for my contemptible behaviour. Secretly, and without a twinge of conscience, I thought what a blessing it would be for _him_ if Heathcliff put him out of his misery, and what a blessing for _me_ if he sent Heathcliff to the place he belonged! While I sat enjoying those thoughts, a blow from Heathcliff knocked the window behind me to the floor, and his dark face appeared through the opening like a curse. The bars were too close together for his shoulders to follow. Thinking myself safe, I smiled in triumph. His hair and clothes were white with snow. His sharp, cannibal teeth, bared by cold and anger, gleamed in the darkness.
“‘Isabella, let me in, or I'll make you sorry!’ he snarled—or ‘girned’, as Joseph calls it.
“‘I can't commit murder,’ I answered. ‘Mr. Hindley is standing guard with a knife and a loaded pistol.’
“‘Open the kitchen door for me,’ he said.

“‘Hindley would get there before me,’ I replied. ‘And what poor love yours is, if it can't stand a shower of snow! While the summer moon shone, we were left in peace in our beds. But the first breath of winter sends you running for shelter! Heathcliff, if I were you I'd lie on her grave and die like a faithful dog. Surely there's nothing left worth living for now? You made it very clear to me that Catherine was all the happiness in your life. I can't imagine how you can think of living after losing her.’
“‘He's there, is he?’ my companion cried, rushing to the opening. ‘If I can get my arm through, I can hit him!’

“I'm afraid you'll think me truly wicked, Ellen. But you don't know everything, so don't judge me. Nothing would have made me help or encourage an attempt even on _his_ life. I couldn't help wishing he were dead, though. So when he threw himself at Earnshaw's weapon and wrenched it from his hand, I was bitterly disappointed, and terrified at what might follow my taunts.

“The pistol went off. The knife sprang back and folded into its owner's wrist. Heathcliff tore it away by brute force, slicing the flesh as he pulled, and thrust the dripping weapon into his pocket. Then he picked up a stone, smashed the dividing bar between two windows, and jumped inside. His opponent had fainted from the terrible pain and the blood pouring from an artery or a large vein. The brute kicked and stamped on him, banging his head against the stone floor again and again. All the while he held me with one hand so I couldn't call Joseph. It took superhuman restraint for him not to finish Hindley altogether, but at last, out of breath, he stopped and dragged the apparently lifeless body on to the bench. He tore off Earnshaw's coat sleeve and roughly bound the wound, spitting and swearing as energetically as he had kicked. Once free, I lost no time in fetching the old servant. Gradually understanding my hurried story, he rushed downstairs, taking the steps two at a time and gasping:
“‘What's to do here now? What's to do here now?’

“‘This is what's happened,’ Heathcliff thundered. ‘Your master's mad. If he lasts another month, I'll have him put in an asylum. And how the devil did you come to lock me out, you toothless hound? Don't stand there muttering and mumbling. Come on, I'm not going to nurse him. Wash that stuff away, and watch the sparks from your candle—it's more than half brandy!’
“‘So ye've been trying to murder him?’ Joseph cried, raising his hands and eyes in horror. ‘Did ever I see such a sight! May the Lord—’

“Heathcliff shoved him to his knees in the blood and threw him a towel. But instead of wiping it up, Joseph clasped his hands and began to pray. His strange choice of words made me laugh. Nothing could shock me in that state of mind. I was as reckless as some criminals are at the foot of the gallows.
“‘Oh, I'd forgotten you,’ the tyrant said. ‘You can do it. Down you go. So you're plotting with him against me, are you, viper? There, that's work fit for you!’

“He shook me until my teeth rattled, then threw me down beside Joseph. Joseph steadily finished his prayers and got up, declaring that he would go straight to the Grange. Mr. Linton was a magistrate, and even if fifty of his wives were dead, he must investigate this. The old man was so determined that Heathcliff thought it best to force me to repeat what had happened. He stood over me, swelling with malice, while I reluctantly answered his questions. It took great effort to convince Joseph that Heathcliff had not begun the attack, especially when every answer had to be dragged from me. Soon, however, Mr. Earnshaw proved that he was still alive. Joseph hurried to give him spirits, and with their help his master began to move and regain his senses. Heathcliff knew his opponent was unaware of what had happened while he was unconscious. He called him deliriously drunk, said he would take no further notice of his outrageous behaviour, and advised him to go to bed. To my delight, after offering this wise counsel, he left us. Hindley stretched out on the hearthstone. I went to my own room, amazed to have escaped so easily.

“This morning I came downstairs about half an hour before noon. Mr. Earnshaw sat by the fire, looking deathly ill, while his tormentor, almost as gaunt and ghastly, leaned against the chimney. Neither seemed inclined to eat. After waiting until everything on the table had gone cold, I began by myself. Nothing stopped me eating heartily. Now and then I glanced at my silent companions with a certain satisfaction and sense of superiority, enjoying the comfort of a clear conscience. When I'd finished, I ventured the unusual freedom of approaching the fire. I went round Earnshaw's chair and knelt in the corner beside him.

“Heathcliff didn't look towards me, and I studied his face almost as confidently as if it had turned to stone. A heavy gloom lay over that forehead I once thought so manly and now find so devilish. His deadly eyes were almost dulled by sleeplessness, and perhaps by crying, for his lashes were wet. His lips had lost their ferocious sneer and were closed in an expression of unspeakable sorrow. Had it been anyone else, I would have covered my face before such grief. With _him_, I was pleased. Ignoble though it may be to insult a fallen enemy, I couldn't miss this chance to wound him. Only when he was weak could I taste the pleasure of repaying one injury with another.”

“Shame, shame, Miss!” I interrupted. “Anyone would think you'd never opened a Bible. If God punishes your enemies, surely that should satisfy you. Adding your own cruelty to his punishment is both mean and presumptuous!”

“Generally I'd agree, Ellen,” she continued. “But what suffering of Heathcliff's could satisfy me unless I had a hand in it? I'd rather he suffered _less_, if I could be the one to cause it and he could _know_ that I was. Oh, I owe him so much. There's only one condition on which I could hope to forgive him: if I could take an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth, return every pang of agony with another, and bring him down to my level. Since he hurt me first, let him be the first to beg forgiveness. Then—well, Ellen, then I might show you some generosity. But I can never possibly have my revenge, so I can never forgive him. Hindley wanted water. I handed him a glass and asked how he felt.
“‘Not as ill as I'd like,’ he answered. ‘But even leaving my arm aside, every inch of me aches as though I'd been fighting a whole army of imps!’

“‘Yes, no wonder,’ I said. ‘Catherine used to boast that she stood between you and physical harm. She meant certain people wouldn't hurt you for fear of offending her. It's a good thing people don't _really_ rise from their graves, or she might have seen a revolting scene last night! Aren't your chest and shoulders covered in cuts and bruises?’
“‘I can't say,’ he answered. ‘But what do you mean? Did he dare to hit me when I was down?’
“‘He stamped on you and kicked you and battered you against the floor,’ I whispered. ‘His mouth watered to tear you with his teeth. He's only half a man—not even that—and all the rest is devil.’

“Like me, Mr. Earnshaw looked up into our common enemy's face. Heathcliff seemed so absorbed in his anguish that he noticed nothing around him. The longer he stood there, the more clearly the darkness of his thoughts showed in his features.

“‘Oh, if God would only give me the strength to strangle him with my dying breath, I'd go to hell gladly,’ the impatient man groaned. He struggled to rise, then sank back in despair, knowing he was too weak for the fight.

“‘No, it's enough that he's murdered one of you,’ I said aloud. ‘Everyone at the Grange knows your sister would be alive now if it weren't for Mr. Heathcliff. After all, being hated by him is better than being loved. When I remember how happy we were—how happy Catherine was before he came—I could curse the day.’

“Heathcliff probably felt the truth of the words more than the malice of the person speaking. I saw that I'd caught his attention. Tears rained from his eyes into the ashes, and he drew breath in choking sighs. I stared straight at him and laughed contemptuously. Those clouded windows of hell flashed towards me for a moment. But the devil that usually looked out of them was so dimmed and drowned that I dared another mocking laugh.
“‘Get up and get out of my sight,’ the grieving man said.
“At least, I believe those were his words, though I could scarcely make out his voice.

“‘I beg your pardon,’ I replied. ‘But I loved Catherine too, and her brother needs looking after. I'll do it for her sake. Now she's dead, I can see her in Hindley. He has exactly her eyes—or would have, if you hadn't tried to gouge them out and made them black and red—and her—’
“‘Get up, you miserable fool, before I stamp you to death!’ he cried. He moved, and that made me move too.

“‘But then,’ I continued, ready to run, ‘if poor Catherine had trusted you and taken that ridiculous, contemptible, degrading title of Mrs. Heathcliff, she would soon have looked the same! _She_ wouldn't have quietly put up with your vile behaviour. She would have found a voice for her hatred and disgust.’

“The back of the bench and Earnshaw himself stood between us. Instead of trying to reach me, Heathcliff seized a dinner knife from the table and threw it at my head. It struck below my ear and cut short what I was saying. I pulled it out, sprang to the door, and threw another remark at him, which I hope went deeper than his knife. My last glimpse was of him rushing furiously towards me, stopped by his host's arms. The two of them fell locked together on the hearth. Running through the kitchen, I told Joseph to hurry to his master. In the doorway I knocked over Hareton, who was hanging a litter of puppies from the back of a chair. Then, blessed as a soul escaped from purgatory, I bounded, leapt, and flew down the steep road. Leaving its bends, I struck straight across the moor, tumbling down banks and wading through marshes, hurling myself towards the guiding light of the Grange. I'd far rather be condemned to live in hell for ever than spend even one more night under the roof of Wuthering Heights.”

Isabella stopped and drank some tea. Then she stood up and asked me to put on her bonnet and the large shawl I had brought. Ignoring my pleas to stay another hour, she climbed on a chair and kissed the portraits of Edgar and Catherine, gave me a kiss too, and went down to the carriage. Fanny followed her, yelping with wild delight at finding her mistress again. She was driven away and never returned to this neighbourhood. Once matters were more settled, however, she and my master began to write regularly. I believe her new home was in the south, near London. A few months after her escape she gave birth there to a son. He was christened Linton, and from the first she described him as sickly and fretful.

One day Mr. Heathcliff met me in the village and asked where she was living. I wouldn't tell him. He said it didn't matter, except that she must be careful not to come to her brother. She should not live with Edgar, even if he had to keep her himself. Although I gave him no information, he discovered her address and the child's existence through other servants. Still, he left her alone; for that restraint she could probably thank his dislike of her. When he saw me, he often asked about the baby. On hearing its name he gave a grim smile and said, “They want me to hate it too, do they?”
“I don't think they want you to know anything about him,” I answered.
“But I'll have him when I want him,” he said. “They can count on that!”
Luckily for his mother, she died before that day came, some thirteen years after Catherine's death, when Linton was twelve or a little older.

The day after Isabella's unexpected visit, I had no chance to speak to my master. He avoided conversation and was in no state to discuss anything. When I finally got him to listen, I could see he was pleased that his sister had left her husband. He hated Heathcliff with an intensity that seemed scarcely possible in someone so gentle. His hatred was so deep and painful that he avoided every place where he might see or hear of him. Together with his grief, it made him a complete recluse. He gave up being a magistrate, stopped even going to church, and stayed away from the village altogether. His life was spent entirely within his park and grounds, broken only by solitary walks on the moors and visits to his wife's grave, usually in the evening or early morning before other people were out. But he was too good to remain utterly unhappy for long. _He_ did not pray for Catherine's spirit to haunt him. Time brought acceptance and a sadness sweeter than ordinary joy. He remembered her with passionate, tender love and looked forward hopefully to the better world where he was certain she had gone.

He had comfort and love on earth as well. For a few days, as I said, he seemed indifferent to the frail little successor to the dead woman. That coldness melted like snow in April. Before the tiny thing could stammer a word or take a stumbling step, she ruled his heart like a tyrant. She was named Catherine, but he never used her full name, just as he had never shortened her mother's—probably because shortening it had been Heathcliff's habit. The little girl was always Cathy. To him, that both distinguished her from her mother and connected them. His love grew far more from her being Catherine's child than from her being his own.

I used to compare him with Hindley Earnshaw and puzzle over why they behaved so differently in similar circumstances. Both had been loving husbands and both cared for their children. I couldn't understand why they had not followed the same road, whether towards good or evil. But I thought Hindley, who seemed the stronger-minded, had proved by far the worse and weaker man. When his ship struck, the captain left his post; instead of trying to save her, the crew fell into riot and confusion, leaving their unlucky vessel without hope. Linton, by contrast, showed the true courage of a loyal, faithful soul. He trusted God, and God comforted him. One hoped and the other despaired. They chose their own fates and were justly made to bear them. But you won't want my moral lessons, Mr. Lockwood. You can judge these things as well as I can—or at least you'll think you can, which comes to the same thing. Earnshaw's end was what one might have expected, and it came soon after his sister's: scarcely six months separated their deaths. We at the Grange never received a very clear account of his condition beforehand. Everything I learnt came when I went to help prepare the funeral. Mr. Kenneth brought the news to my master.
“Well, Nelly,” he said, riding into the yard one morning so early that I immediately feared bad news, “it's your turn and mine to go into mourning. Who do you think has slipped away from us now?”
“Who?” I asked in alarm.
“Go on, guess!” he answered, getting down and hanging his bridle on the hook beside the door. “And get the corner of your apron ready. I'm certain you'll need it.”
“Surely not Mr. Heathcliff?” I cried.

“What! Would you shed tears for him?” the doctor said. “No, Heathcliff's a tough young fellow. He's looking splendid today; I've just seen him. He's putting on flesh quickly since he lost his better half.”
“Then who is it, Mr. Kenneth?” I asked again, impatiently.

“Hindley Earnshaw! Your old friend Hindley,” he answered, “and my wicked drinking companion, though he's been too wild for me for a long time. There! I knew we'd start the tears. But take heart! He died true to form, drunk as a lord. Poor lad! I'm sorry too. You can't help missing an old companion, even one with the worst tricks a man ever thought of, who's played me many a scurvy turn. It seems he was barely twenty-seven, the same age as you. Who'd have guessed you were born in the same year?”

I confess this was a harder blow to me than Mrs. Linton's death. Old memories still clung round my heart. I sat down in the porch and wept as though for a blood relation, asking Mr. Kenneth to find another servant to take him to the master. I couldn't keep one question out of my mind: “Had he been fairly treated?” Whatever I did, that thought troubled me. It persisted so wearisomely that I decided to ask leave to go to Wuthering Heights and help with the final duties to the dead. Mr. Linton was very reluctant to agree. I pleaded earnestly that Hindley lay there friendless, and that my former master and foster brother had as strong a claim on my help as he did. I also reminded him that Hareton was his wife's nephew. With no closer relative present, he ought to act as the boy's guardian, find out how the property stood, and examine his brother-in-law's affairs. He was in no condition to handle such matters himself, but told me to speak to his lawyer and at last allowed me to go. The lawyer had also acted for Earnshaw. I called on him in the village and asked him to accompany me. He shook his head and advised leaving Heathcliff alone, saying that if the truth were known, Hareton would prove little better than a beggar.

“His father died in debt,” he said. “The entire property is mortgaged. The rightful heir's only chance is to be allowed to awaken some affection in the creditor, so that he may be disposed to treat him generously.”

When I reached the Heights, I explained that I had come to make sure everything was done decently. Joseph, who seemed quite distressed, was pleased to see me. Mr. Heathcliff said he didn't see any need for me, but I could stay and organise the funeral if I wished.

“Properly speaking,” he remarked, “that fool's body ought to be buried at a crossroads without any ceremony. Yesterday afternoon I happened to leave him for ten minutes. In that time he locked both doors against me, then spent the night deliberately drinking himself to death! We broke in this morning because we heard him snorting like a horse. There he lay across the bench. You could have skinned and scalped him without waking him. I sent for Kenneth, who came—but not before the beast had turned to carrion. He was dead, cold, and stiff, so you must agree there was no point making any more fuss about him!”
The old servant backed up this account, but muttered:
“I'd sooner he'd gone for t' doctor himself! I'd have looked after master better than he did. And he weren't dead when I left—nowt o' t' sort!”

I insisted on a respectable funeral. Mr. Heathcliff said I could have my way about that too, provided I remembered that he was paying for the whole business. His manner remained hard and indifferent, showing neither joy nor grief. If anything, it suggested a stony satisfaction at having successfully completed a difficult task. Once, though, I did see something like triumph in his face: just as the coffin was being carried out. He had the hypocrisy to play the mourner. Before following with Hareton, he lifted the unfortunate child on to the table and muttered with particular relish, “Now, my bonny lad, you're _mine_! We'll see whether one tree won't grow as crooked as another when the same wind twists it!” The unsuspecting child was pleased. He played with Heathcliff's whiskers and stroked his cheek. But I understood the meaning and said sharply, “That boy must come back with me to Thrushcross Grange, sir. Nothing in the world belongs to you less than he does!”
“Is that what Linton says?” he demanded.
“Of course. He's told me to bring him,” I answered.

“Well,” the scoundrel said, “we won't argue about it now. But I fancy trying my hand at bringing up a child. Tell your master that if he tries to take this one away, I'll have to replace him with my own. I'm not promising to let Hareton go without a fight, but I'll make quite sure the other one comes! Remember to tell him.”

That threat was enough to tie our hands. I repeated its substance when I returned. Edgar Linton, who had shown little interest to begin with, said no more about intervening. I don't know that he could have achieved anything even if he had been eager to try.

The guest had now become master of Wuthering Heights. He took secure possession and proved to the lawyer, who in turn proved to Mr. Linton, that Earnshaw had mortgaged every yard of his land to finance his obsession with gambling. Heathcliff held the mortgage. In this way Hareton, who ought now to be the leading gentleman in the neighbourhood, became entirely dependent on his father's bitterest enemy. He lives in his own house as an unpaid servant, quite unable to put matters right, because he has no friends to help him and does not even know he has been wronged.

chapters.title: Chapter XVIII
paragraphs: The twelve years after that miserable time, Mrs. Dean continued, were the happiest of my life. My greatest worries were the minor illnesses our little lady suffered, like every child, rich or poor. Otherwise, after her first six months, she grew like a larch tree. Before the heather flowered for the second time over Mrs. Linton's grave, she could walk and, in her own fashion, talk. No more delightful creature ever brought sunshine into a desolate house. She was truly beautiful, with the Earnshaws' handsome dark eyes, but the Lintons' fair skin and small features, and curling golden hair. She was spirited without being rough, and her sensitive heart overflowed with lively affection. Her capacity for deep attachment reminded me of her mother, but otherwise she was different. She could be as gentle and mild as a dove, with a soft voice and a thoughtful expression. Her anger never became fury, and her love was deep and tender, never fierce. Still, she had faults to set against her gifts. One was a tendency to be cheeky; another was the wilfulness that all indulged children acquire, whether good-tempered or cross. If a servant displeased her, it was always, “I'll tell papa!” If he reproved her, even with a look, you would have thought her heart was breaking. I don't believe he ever spoke a harsh word to her. He took full charge of her education and made it a pleasure. Fortunately she was curious and quick-minded, so she learnt eagerly and rapidly, doing credit to his teaching.

Until she was thirteen, she had never once gone beyond the park on her own. On rare occasions Mr. Linton took her a mile or so farther, but he would trust her to nobody else. Gimmerton was only a vague name to her. Apart from her home, the chapel was the only building she had ever approached or entered. Wuthering Heights and Mr. Heathcliff did not exist for her. She lived in complete seclusion and seemed perfectly content. Sometimes, though, looking out over the country from her nursery window, she would say:
“Ellen, how long before I can walk to the tops of those hills? I wonder what's beyond them. Is it the sea?”
“No, Miss Cathy,” I would tell her. “There are more hills, just like these.”
“And what do those golden rocks look like when you're underneath them?” she once asked.

The steep face of Penistone Crags particularly caught her attention, especially when the setting sun lit it and the highest peaks while all the rest of the landscape lay in shadow. I explained that they were bare masses of rock, with scarcely enough soil in their cracks to support a stunted tree.
“Why do they stay bright so long after it's evening here?” she went on.

“Because they're so much higher than we are,” I replied. “You couldn't climb them; they're too high and steep. In winter the frost always reaches them before us. I've even found snow well into summer beneath that dark hollow on the northeast side!”
“Oh, you've been up there!” she cried in delight. “Then I can go too when I'm a woman. Has papa been, Ellen?”

“Papa would tell you, Miss,” I answered quickly, “that they're not worth the trouble of a visit. The moors where you walk with him are much nicer, and Thrushcross Park is the finest place in the world.”
“But I know the park, and I don't know those,” she murmured to herself. “I'd love to look round from the very top of the highest one. My little pony Minny shall take me one day.”

When a maid mentioned the Fairy Cave, she became wild with eagerness to make the journey. She pestered Mr. Linton until he promised to take her when she was older. But Miss Catherine measured her age in months and was always asking, “Am I old enough to go to Penistone Crags now?” The road passed close to Wuthering Heights, and Edgar could not bear to go past it. So the answer was always the same: “Not yet, love. Not yet.”

As I said, Mrs. Heathcliff lived more than twelve years after leaving her husband. Her family had delicate constitutions; neither she nor Edgar had the robust, rosy health usual in these parts. I'm not certain what her last illness was. I suspect they both died of the same thing, a kind of fever that began slowly but was incurable and rapidly consumed them towards the end. After being ill for four months, she wrote to her brother explaining how it was likely to end and begging him to come if he could. She had much to arrange, wanted to say goodbye, and wished to place Linton safely in his hands. She hoped the boy might be left with Edgar as he had been left with her. She tried to persuade herself that his father had no wish to take on the expense of maintaining or educating him. My master did not hesitate. Reluctant as he usually was to leave home, he hurried to answer this call. He put Catherine under my particular care while he was away, repeatedly ordering that she must not go beyond the park, even with me. It never occurred to him that she might go alone.

He was away for three weeks. For the first day or two my charge sat in a corner of the library, too sad to read or play. While she was quiet she gave me little trouble. But then she grew restless, fretful, and bored. I was too busy, and by then too old, to run about entertaining her, so I found a way for her to amuse herself. I sent her on journeys round the grounds, sometimes on foot, sometimes on her pony, and patiently listened to all her real and imaginary adventures when she came back.

Summer was at its height. She grew so fond of wandering alone that she often managed to stay out from breakfast until tea, then spent the evening telling her fanciful stories. I didn't fear that she would cross the boundaries. The gates were usually locked, and I thought she would hardly venture out alone even if they stood wide open. Unfortunately, my confidence was misplaced. One morning at eight Catherine told me that today she was an Arabian merchant crossing the desert with his caravan. I must give her plenty of provisions for herself and her animals: one horse and three camels, represented by a large hound and two pointers. I gathered a generous supply of treats and hung the basket on one side of her saddle. She sprang up, merry as a fairy, protected from the July sun by a broad-brimmed hat and gauze veil. Laughing at my cautious warnings not to gallop and to come home early, she trotted away. The naughty creature never appeared for tea. One traveller, the hound, came back: he was old and liked his comfort. But there was no sign anywhere of Cathy, the pony, or the two pointers. I sent people down one path and another, then went searching myself. At the edge of the grounds a labourer was repairing a fence round a plantation. I asked whether he had seen our young lady.
“I saw her this morning,” he replied. “She asked me to cut her a hazel switch, then jumped her pony over that hedge where it's lowest and galloped out of sight.”

You can imagine how I felt. At once I guessed she had set off for Penistone Crags. “What will become of her?” I cried, pushing through the gap the man was mending and heading straight for the main road. I walked as though racing for a prize, mile after mile, until a bend brought the Heights into view. But nowhere, near or far, could I see Catherine. The Crags lie about a mile and a half beyond Mr. Heathcliff's house, itself four miles from the Grange. I began to fear it would be dark before I reached them. “What if she's slipped while climbing and been killed, or broken a bone?” I thought. The uncertainty was agonising. At first, therefore, I was wonderfully relieved when, hurrying past the farmhouse, I saw Charlie, the fiercer pointer, lying beneath a window with a swollen head and a bleeding ear. I opened the little gate, ran to the door, and knocked hard. A woman I knew from Gimmerton answered. She had been a servant there since Mr. Earnshaw died.
“Ah,” she said, “you've come looking for your little mistress! Don't worry, she's safe here. But I'm glad it isn't the master.”
“He isn't at home, then?” I panted, breathless from alarm and my hurried walk.
“No, no,” she answered. “He and Joseph are both out, and I don't expect them back for another hour or more. Come in and rest a little.”

I went in and found my straying lamb beside the hearth, rocking in the little chair that had belonged to her mother as a child. Her hat hung on the wall, and she seemed entirely at home, laughing and chattering in excellent spirits to Hareton. He was now a tall, strong lad of eighteen. He stared at her with great curiosity and astonishment, understanding very little of the endless stream of remarks and questions pouring from her tongue.
“Very well, Miss!” I exclaimed, hiding my joy behind an angry face. “That's your last ride until papa comes home. I won't trust you outside the door again, you naughty, naughty girl!”
“Aha, Ellen!” she cried merrily, jumping up and running to me. “What a story I'll have tonight! So you've found me. Have you ever been here before in your life?”

“Put your hat on and come home at once,” I said. “I'm terribly disappointed in you, Miss Cathy. You've behaved very badly! Pouting and crying won't undo all the trouble I've had searching the countryside. To think how Mr. Linton charged me to keep you at home, and then you slipped away like this! It shows you're a cunning little fox. Nobody will trust you again.”
“What have I done?” she sobbed, her happiness instantly crushed. “Papa didn't tell me anything. He won't scold me, Ellen. He's never cross like you!”
“Come along, come along!” I repeated. “I'll tie your ribbon. Now, no sulking. Oh, shame on you! Thirteen years old and still such a baby!”
I said this because she had pushed off the hat and retreated to the fireplace, out of my reach.

“Nay,” the servant said, “don't be hard on the bonny lass, Mrs. Dean. We made her stay. She wanted to ride on because she feared you'd worry. Hareton offered to go with her, and I thought he ought to; it's a wild road over the hills.”
Throughout this exchange Hareton stood with his hands in his pockets, too awkward to speak, though he plainly disliked my intrusion.

“How long must I wait?” I went on, ignoring the woman's interference. “It'll be dark in ten minutes. Where's the pony, Miss Cathy? And where's Phoenix? If you don't hurry, I'll leave you. Please yourself.”
“The pony's in the yard,” she answered, “and Phoenix is shut in there. He's been bitten, and so has Charlie. I was going to tell you everything, but you're in a bad temper and don't deserve to hear.”

I picked up her hat and went to put it on again. Seeing that the household took her side, she began skipping round the room. When I chased her, she darted like a mouse over, under, and behind the furniture until pursuing her made me ridiculous. Hareton and the woman laughed. She joined in and grew still more cheeky, until I cried in great irritation, “Well, Miss Cathy, if you knew whose house this was, you'd be glad enough to leave!”
“It's _your_ father's house, isn't it?” she asked, turning to Hareton.
“Nay,” he said, looking down with an embarrassed blush.
He could not bear her steady gaze, though her eyes were just like his own.
“Then whose is it? Your master's?” she asked.
He flushed more deeply, this time for another reason, muttered a curse, and turned away.

“Who is his master?” the troublesome girl asked me. “He kept saying ‘our house’ and ‘our folk’. I thought he was the owner's son. And he never called me Miss. He should have, shouldn't he, if he's a servant?”
At this childish speech Hareton's face darkened like a thundercloud. Without speaking, I shook her and finally managed to get her ready to go.

“Now fetch my horse,” she told her unrecognised relative, just as she would address a stable boy at the Grange. “And you can come with me. I want to see where the goblin-hunter comes up in the marsh, and hear about the _fairishes_, as you call them. But hurry! What's wrong? Fetch my horse, I said.”
“I'll see thee damned before I'll be _thy_ servant!” the lad growled.
“You'll see me _what_?” Catherine asked in astonishment.
“Damned, thou cheeky witch!” he answered.
“There, Miss Cathy! You see what fine company you've found,” I put in. “What lovely language to use to a young lady! Please don't start arguing with him. Come, we'll find Minny ourselves and go.”
“But Ellen,” she cried, staring in astonishment, “how dare he speak to me like that? Shouldn't he be made to do what I ask? You wicked creature, I'll tell papa what you said. There!”
Hareton seemed unmoved by this threat, and tears of indignation sprang to her eyes. “You fetch the pony,” she told the woman, “and let my dog out this instant!”
“Gently, Miss,” the woman replied. “Being polite won't hurt you. Mr. Hareton here may not be the master's son, but he's your cousin. And I wasn't hired to serve you.”
“_Him_, my cousin!” Cathy cried with a scornful laugh.
“Yes, indeed he is,” the woman who had corrected her answered.

“Oh, Ellen! Don't let them say things like that,” she went on, deeply distressed. “Papa's gone to London to fetch my cousin. My cousin is a gentleman's son. That creature my—” She stopped and burst into tears, upset by the very idea of being related to such a boor.
“Hush, hush!” I whispered. “People can have many cousins, of every sort, Miss Cathy, without being any the worse for it. They needn't spend time with them if they're unpleasant and badly behaved.”
“He isn't—he isn't my cousin, Ellen!” she insisted. Thinking about it only made her more miserable, and she threw herself into my arms to escape the idea.

I was thoroughly annoyed with both her and the servant for what each had revealed. I had no doubt that Cathy's news of Linton's coming arrival would reach Mr. Heathcliff. I was just as certain that, when her father returned, Catherine's first thought would be to ask him to explain the woman's claim about her uncouth relation. Hareton, recovering from his anger at being mistaken for a servant, seemed touched by her distress. He fetched the pony to the door, then took a handsome bow-legged terrier puppy from the kennel as a peace offering. Placing it in her hands, he told her, “Hush! I meant no harm.” She paused in her crying to look at him with awe and horror, then started again.

I could hardly help smiling at her dislike of the poor fellow. He was a well-built, athletic youth, strong, healthy, and good-looking, though dressed for his daily work on the farm and his idle hunting of rabbits and game across the moors. I thought I could see in his face signs of better qualities than his father had ever possessed. Good qualities lost in a wilderness of weeds, certainly, with the rank weeds towering above their neglected growth; still, they showed rich soil that might have yielded a fine harvest in better circumstances. I believe Mr. Heathcliff had not physically mistreated him. His fearless nature offered no temptation to that kind of cruelty: he had none of the timid sensitivity that would have made abuse enjoyable to Heathcliff. Instead, Heathcliff seemed to have directed his malice towards making him a brute. He was never taught to read or write, never corrected for a bad habit unless it annoyed his keeper, never guided one step towards goodness or warned against wrongdoing. From what I heard, Joseph did much to make him worse. His narrow loyalty to the old family led him to flatter and spoil Hareton as a boy because he was its head. When Catherine Earnshaw and Heathcliff were children, Joseph had blamed their ‘awful ways’ for driving their master beyond patience and forcing him to seek comfort in drink. Now he blamed every fault in Hareton on the man who had taken his property. He would not correct the lad for swearing, or for any other misconduct, however bad. Apparently it pleased him to see Hareton go to the greatest extremes. He admitted the boy was ruined and his soul abandoned to damnation, but then reflected that Heathcliff would have to answer for it. Hareton's blood would be required at Heathcliff's hands, and that thought gave Joseph enormous comfort. He had taught Hareton pride in his name and ancestry. Had he dared, he would have encouraged hatred between him and the present owner of the Heights, but his fear of that owner was almost superstitious. He confined his feelings to muttered hints and private curses. I don't claim to know closely how life was lived at Wuthering Heights in those days. I saw little and can only report what I heard. The villagers called Mr. Heathcliff miserly, a cruel and harsh landlord. But with a woman managing it, the house had regained its old comfort, and the drunken disorders of Hindley's day no longer took place within its walls. Its master was too gloomy to want anyone's company, good or bad. He still is.

But this isn't getting on with my story. Miss Cathy refused the terrier offered in peace and demanded her own dogs, Charlie and Phoenix. They came limping with their heads down, and we set off home, all of us thoroughly out of sorts. I could get little from my young lady about her day, except that, as I had supposed, she had set out for Penistone Crags. She reached the farmhouse gate without incident just as Hareton came out with several dogs, which attacked hers. A sharp fight followed before the owners could separate them, and this introduced the pair. Catherine told Hareton who she was and where she was going, asked him the way, and finally persuaded him to accompany her. He showed her the mysteries of the Fairy Cave and twenty other strange places. But since I was out of favour, I received no description of these wonders. I gathered that she had liked her guide very much until she hurt his feelings by treating him as a servant, and Heathcliff's housekeeper hurt hers by calling him her cousin. His words still rankled. She was always ‘love’, ‘darling’, ‘queen’, and ‘angel’ to everyone at the Grange, and now a stranger had insulted her so dreadfully! She couldn't understand it. It took hard work to get her promise not to complain to her father. I explained how he disliked everyone at the Heights and how unhappy he would be to learn she had gone there. Most of all, I stressed that if she revealed my failure to obey his orders, he might be so angry that I would have to leave. Cathy couldn't bear that prospect. She gave her word and kept it for my sake. After all, she was a sweet little girl.

chapters.title: Chapter XIX
paragraphs: A black-bordered letter told us when my master would return. Isabella was dead. He asked me to arrange mourning clothes for his daughter and prepare a room and everything else needed for his young nephew. Catherine was wild with joy at the thought of her father's homecoming and imagined countless wonderful qualities in her ‘real’ cousin. The evening of their expected arrival came. She had been busy arranging her little affairs since early morning. Now, dressed in her new black frock—poor thing! Her aunt's death meant no definite sorrow to her—she pestered me until I agreed to walk down through the grounds to meet them.

“Linton is only six months younger than me,” she chattered as we walked slowly over the mossy rises and hollows beneath the trees. “What fun it will be to have him to play with! Aunt Isabella sent papa a beautiful lock of his hair. It was lighter than mine, more like flax, and just as fine. I keep it carefully in a little glass box. I've often thought how lovely it would be to see the boy it belongs to. Oh! I'm so happy—and papa, dear, dear papa! Come on, Ellen, let's run! Come, run.”

She ran ahead, came back, and ran off again many times before my steady footsteps brought me to the gate. Then she sat on the grassy bank beside the path and tried to wait patiently. But it was impossible: she couldn't keep still for a minute.

“How long they're taking!” she cried. “Ah, there's dust on the road—they're coming! No! When will they get here? Couldn't we go a little farther? Half a mile, Ellen, only half a mile? Do say yes—as far as those birch trees at the bend!”

I firmly refused. At last her waiting ended: the travelling carriage came into view. As soon as she saw her father's face at the window, Miss Cathy shrieked and held out her arms. He got down almost as eagerly as she ran to him, and for quite a while they thought of nobody but each other. While they exchanged kisses, I looked inside for Linton. He was asleep in a corner, wrapped in a warm fur-lined cloak as though it were winter. He was a pale, delicate, girlish boy, so like my master that he might have been his younger brother. But there was a sickly fretfulness in his face that Edgar Linton had never had. Edgar saw me looking, shook my hand, and asked me to close the door and leave him undisturbed, since the journey had exhausted him. Cathy wanted a glimpse too, but her father called her away. They walked together up the park while I hurried ahead to prepare the servants.

“Now, darling,” Mr. Linton said to his daughter as they stopped at the foot of the front steps, “your cousin isn't as strong or as cheerful as you are. Remember that he has only just lost his mother. So don't expect him to run about and play with you straight away. And don't tire him with too much talking. Let him have a quiet evening, at least, will you?”
“Yes, yes, papa,” Catherine answered. “But I do want to see him, and he hasn't looked out even once.”
The carriage stopped. The sleeping boy was woken, and his uncle lifted him down.

“This is your cousin Cathy, Linton,” he said, joining their small hands. “She's fond of you already. Don't upset her by crying tonight. Try to be cheerful. The journey's over now, and all you need to do is rest and enjoy yourself however you like.”
“Then let me go to bed,” the boy answered, shrinking away from Catherine's greeting. He pressed his fingers to his eyes to wipe away the tears forming there.
“Come now, be a good child,” I whispered as I led him in. “You'll make her cry too. Look how sorry she feels for you!”

Whether it was pity for him I cannot say, but his cousin looked just as unhappy as he did and went back to her father. All three came inside and went up to the library, where tea was ready. I took off Linton's cap and cloak and put him in a chair at the table. No sooner had he sat down than he started crying again. My master asked what was wrong.
“I can't sit in a chair,” the boy sobbed.
“Then lie on the sofa, and Ellen will bring you tea,” his uncle answered patiently.

I felt sure that this fretful, sickly child had tried his patience severely on the journey. Linton dragged himself slowly across the room and lay down. Cathy brought a footstool and her cup to his side. At first she sat quietly, but that couldn't last. She had decided to make a pet of her little cousin, as she insisted on thinking him. She began stroking his curls, kissing his cheek, and offering him tea from her saucer as though he were a baby. This pleased him, for he was little better than one. He dried his eyes and managed a faint smile.

“Oh, he'll do very well,” the master said to me after watching them briefly. “Very well, if we can keep him, Ellen. Having a child his own age for company will soon give him new spirit. Once he wants to be strong, he'll grow stronger.”

“Yes, if we can keep him!” I thought, with a dreadful suspicion that there was little hope of it. How could that weak little creature live at Wuthering Heights? What playmates and teachers his father and Hareton would make! Our uncertainty ended even sooner than I expected. After tea I took the children upstairs and stayed until Linton fell asleep; he would not let me leave before that. I had just come down and was standing at the hall table, lighting a bedroom candle for Mr. Edgar, when a maid came out of the kitchen. Mr. Heathcliff's servant Joseph was at the door, she said, and wanted to speak to the master.
“I'll find out what he wants first,” I said, considerably alarmed. “What an odd hour to trouble people, just as they've returned from a long journey. I don't think the master can see him.”

While I spoke, Joseph had come through the kitchen and now stood in the hall. He wore his Sunday clothes and his sourest, most pious expression. With his hat in one hand and his stick in the other, he began wiping his shoes on the mat.
“Good evening, Joseph,” I said coldly. “What brings you here tonight?”
“It's Master Linton I mun speak to,” he answered, waving me contemptuously aside.
“Mr. Linton is going to bed,” I continued. “Unless it's something especially important, I'm sure he won't hear it tonight. You'd better sit down in there and give me your message.”
“Which is his room?” the man persisted, looking along the row of closed doors.

I saw that he was determined not to deal through me. Very reluctantly I went up to the library, announced the late visitor, and advised sending him away until morning. Mr. Linton had no time to authorise this: Joseph followed close behind me and pushed into the room. Planting himself on the far side of the table, both fists on the head of his stick, he began loudly, as though already expecting resistance:
“Heathcliff's sent me for his lad, and I munn't go back without him.”

Edgar Linton was silent for a moment. Deep sorrow spread over his face. He would have pitied the child for his own sake, but remembering Isabella's hopes and fears, her anxious wishes for her son, and how she had entrusted him to his care, he grieved bitterly at the thought of surrendering him. He searched his heart for a way to prevent it, but could find none. Any sign that he wanted to keep the boy would only make Heathcliff more insistent. There was nothing to do but give him up. Still, he would not wake him from sleep.

“Tell Mr. Heathcliff,” he answered calmly, “that his son will come to Wuthering Heights tomorrow. He's in bed and far too tired to travel that distance tonight. You may also tell him that Linton's mother wished him to remain in my care, and that his health is very uncertain at present.”

“Nay!” Joseph said, thumping his stick on the floor and taking an air of authority. “Nay! That counts for nowt. Heathcliff takes no heed o' t' mother, nor thee either. But he'll have his lad, and I mun take him. Now ye know!”
“You will not take him tonight!” Linton answered firmly. “Go downstairs at once and repeat what I've told you to your master. Ellen, show him out. Go—”
Taking the indignant old man by the arm, he helped him out of the room and shut the door.
“Very well!” Joseph shouted as he slowly withdrew. “Tomorrow he'll come himself. Put _him_ out, if ye dare!”

chapters.title: Chapter XX
paragraphs: To prevent that threat from being carried out, Mr. Linton instructed me to take the boy to his father's early, on Catherine's pony. “Since we can no longer influence his fate for better or worse,” he said, “you mustn't tell my daughter where he's gone. She cannot see him again, and it's better that she doesn't know how close he is, or she'll become restless and want to visit the Heights. Simply say that his father sent for him unexpectedly and he had to leave us.”

Linton hated being woken at five o'clock and was astonished to hear that he must get ready to travel again. I tried to soften the news by saying he was going to spend some time with his father, Mr. Heathcliff, who wanted to see him so much that he couldn't wait until the boy had recovered from his last journey.
“My father!” he cried, looking utterly puzzled. “Mamma never told me I had a father. Where does he live? I'd rather stay with uncle.”

“He lives not far from the Grange,” I answered, “just beyond those hills. It's close enough for you to walk over here when you're stronger. You ought to be glad to go home and see him. Try to love him as you loved your mother, and then he'll love you.”
“But why have I never heard about him?” Linton asked. “Why didn't he and mamma live together like other people?”
“His business kept him in the north,” I replied, “and your mother's health meant she had to live in the south.”
“But why didn't mamma tell me about him?” the child persisted. “She often talked about uncle, and I learnt to love him long ago. How can I love papa? I don't know him.”

“Oh, all children love their parents,” I said. “Perhaps your mother thought you'd want to be with him if she spoke of him often. Let's hurry. An early ride on such a beautiful morning is much nicer than another hour in bed.”
“Is _she_ coming with us?” he asked. “The little girl I saw yesterday?”
“Not this time,” I answered.
“Is uncle coming?” he went on.
“No, I'm taking you there,” I said.
Linton fell back on his pillow and lay deep in thought.
“I won't go without uncle,” he said at last. “I don't know where you're going to take me.”

I tried to persuade him that it was naughty to be unwilling to meet his father. Still he stubbornly refused to begin dressing, and I had to call my master to help coax him out of bed. Eventually we got the poor child away by falsely assuring him that he would not be gone long and that Mr. Edgar and Cathy would visit. I invented other equally unfounded promises and repeated them from time to time throughout the journey. After a while, the clean, heather-scented air, bright sunshine, and Minny's gentle canter lifted his spirits. He began asking about his new home and the people there with greater interest and liveliness.
“Is Wuthering Heights as nice as Thrushcross Grange?” he asked, turning for a last look into the valley, where a thin mist was rising to form a fleecy cloud at the edge of the blue sky.

“It isn't so hidden among trees,” I answered, “and it's not quite as big. But it has beautiful views of the whole countryside, and the air is healthier for you, fresher and drier. At first you may think the building old and dark, though it's a respectable house, the next best in the neighbourhood. And you'll have lovely walks on the moors. Hareton Earnshaw—that's Miss Cathy's other cousin, and in a way yours—will show you all the nicest places. In fine weather you can bring a book and make a green hollow your study. Now and then your uncle may join you for a walk. He often walks on the hills.”
“What does my father look like?” he asked. “Is he as young and handsome as uncle?”

“He's as young,” I said, “but his hair and eyes are black, and he looks sterner. He's taller and bigger altogether. At first he may not seem as gentle and kind, because that isn't his manner. But remember to be open and affectionate with him. Naturally he'll love you more than any uncle, because you're his own child.”
“Black hair and eyes!” Linton said thoughtfully. “I can't imagine him. Then I don't look like him, do I?”

“Not much,” I replied. Not in the least, I thought, looking sadly at my companion's pale complexion, slender body, and large, languid eyes. They were his mother's eyes, except that they held no trace of her lively sparkle unless an unhealthy irritability briefly lit them.
“How strange that he never came to see mamma and me!” he murmured. “Has he ever seen me? If he has, I must have been a baby. I can't remember a single thing about him!”

“Well, Master Linton,” I said, “three hundred miles is a long way. And ten years seems a very different length of time to a grown person than it does to you. Mr. Heathcliff probably planned to come summer after summer but never found a convenient opportunity. Now it's too late. Don't question him about it; you'll only upset him for no good reason.”

The boy remained absorbed in his thoughts for the rest of the ride, until we stopped at the farmhouse garden gate. I watched his face to see what he thought. He solemnly studied the carved front, the low windows, the straggling gooseberry bushes, and the crooked firs, then shook his head. Inwardly he thoroughly disliked the outside of his new home. But he had the sense to hold back his complaints: there might be something better inside. Before he dismounted, I went to open the door. It was half past six.
